#9468. Physician Burnout by Specialty & Other Physician Mental Health Statistics

In the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, physicians continue to experience burnout at alarmingly high rates. In a recent survey of 2440 physicians, approximately 63% of respondents reported having at least 1 manifestation of burnout in 2021; this was higher than all 4 prior assessment time points since 2011.1 Because physician burnout is more common in certain specialties, it is crucial to identify trends and offer help to those at higher risk. This article examines the symptoms, causes, and prevalence of burnout among clinicians in various specialties, and outlines strategies physicians can use to address burnout.

The American Medical Association (AMA) defines physician burnout as a long-term stress reaction that can include the following2:

For many clinicians, symptoms of burnout were accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic. During the pandemic, chronic stress due to work overload, exposure to infected patients, lack of protective equipment, and poor efforts to control infection rates increased the risk of burnout.3 Other factors associated with burnout include system inefficiencies, administrative burdens, and increased regulation and technology requirements.2

The consequences of physician burnout affect patients as well as clinicians. From a patient’s perspective, physician burnout can result in poor physician/patient rapport, adherence to treatment, and treatment outcomes.4 For physicians, burnout can lead to declining mental health and subsequent depression, substance abuse, and suicide.4

Although burnout affects clinicians in all specialties and practice settings, the rate is higher in certain specialties. The AMA’s Organization Biopsy® is an assessment tool large health care organizations can use to measure and improve the health of their organizations.5 One of the parameters this tool measures is burnout.

The AMA’s 2022 Organizational Biopsy received more than 13,000 responses from physicians and other clinicians from more than 70 organizations in 30 states. The specialties with the highest rates of burnout were as follows6:

Medscape conducts an annual survey on physician lifestyle and happiness that includes questions about burnout and depression. In 2023, this 10-minute online survey included input from 9,175 physicians in 29 specialties.7 Overall for all specialties, 36% of respondents said they felt burned out, 5% said they felt depressed, and 18% said they felt both burned out and depressed.8 Based on the Medscape 2023 survey results, the following sections summarize the rates of burnout and depression among physicians clinicians working in emergency medicine, family medicine, pediatrics, obstetrics and gynecology, and internal medicine.

In Medscape’s 2023 survey, emergency physicians reported the following8:

Burnout was reported by a higher proportion of women (51%) than men (38%). The 3 largest factors contributing to burnout among emergency medicine physicians were having too many bureaucratic tasks (51%), a lack of respect from patients (50%), and a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (46%).8

Slightly more than one-half of female family physicians (51%) and one-third of male family physicians (33%) reported experiencing burnout.9 The overall proportion of respondents who said they felt burned out was 42%. Depression affected 4% of family medicine physicians, while 15% said they felt both burned out and depressed.9

By far the largest contributor to family physician burnout was having too many bureaucratic tasks; 73% of respondents reported tasks such as paperwork and charting were the main culprit. Working too many hours and a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff were cited as factors contributing to burnout by 36% and 31% of respondents, respectively.9

Overall, 39% of pediatricians reported feeling burned out.11 More female pediatricians reported feeling burned out more than their male counterparts (46% vs 26%, respectively).10 The proportion of respondents who said they felt depressed was 3%, while 19% reported being both burned out and depressed.

The 3 largest contributors to burnout were having too many bureaucratic tasks (65%), lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (40%), and spending too many hours at work (38%).10

In Medscape’s 2023 report, obstetrics and gynecology physicians reported the following11:

Obstetrics and gynecology physicians reported that the 3 largest contributors to their burnout were having too many bureaucratic tasks (56%), spending too many hours at work (47%), and a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (42%).11

Nearly half of female internists (49%) reported dealing with burnout, vs 31% of male internists.12 However, 4% of both male and female internists said they felt depressed, and 21% of both male and female internists said they felt both burned out and depressed.12

Having too many bureaucratic tasks was the primary contributor to internist burnout (64%). Insufficient compensation/salary was the second-leading factor (40%), followed by a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (35%).12

#9466. Study: Menstrual Cycle Irregularities Linked to ADHD, Depression, Anxiety in Girls

Menstrual cycle irregularities, like severe menstrual pain and premenstrual symptoms, are associated with mental health conditions in adolescent girls, according to a new study.

Several menstrual cycle characteristics, including timing of menarche, cycle regularity, menstrual pain, and severity of premenstrual symptoms, are associated with more common and severe symptoms of depression, anxiety, and ADHD in adolescent girls, according to a recent study published in European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry.1

The longitudinal study followed 5,673 adolescent girls, ages 9 to 11, over a seven-year period, with annual assessments up to ages 14 to 17.

Study participants self-reported the severity of premenstrual symptoms, such as irritability and fatigue, and the intensity of period pain (categorized as mild, moderate, or severe). Findings showed that severe menstrual pain was associated with higher anxiety, depression, and ADHD symptoms.

Premenstrual symptoms demonstrated a graded pattern in their association with mental health outcomes. Mild premenstrual symptoms were linked to higher anxiety symptom scores. Moderate premenstrual symptoms were linked to higher anxiety and depression symptom scores. Severe premenstrual symptoms were linked to higher anxiety, depression, and ADHD symptom scores.

The researchers offered several social and biological factors as potential explanations for these results.

“Psychosocially, menstrual pain and [premenstrual symptoms] may result in functional impairment – including missed school, disrupted sleep, reduced social participation – which may contribute to emotional distress,” they wrote.

The study explained that intense period pain and premenstrual distress may activate inflammatory and pain-sensitivity pathways, increasing vulnerability to anxiety and depression. Researchers also noted that the neurobiological mechanisms for processing pain may overlap with those involved in attention and focus, which could help explain the connection between menstrual pain and ADHD symptoms.

Researchers also suggested that fluctuating estrogen and progesterone may help to explain the connection between severe premenstrual symptoms and higher anxiety, depression, and ADHD symptom scores. These hormones heavily affect serotonin, dopamine, and GABA in the brain. Serotonin is linked to mood; dopamine controls motivation and reward processing; and GABA is crucial for emotional processing and regulation. When hormones fluctuate before a menstrual cycle, these neurotransmitters are impacted too, which, in turn, may influence symptoms of anxiety, depression, and ADHD.

The relationship between ADHD and hormonal fluctuations is a pressing subject for many ADDitude readers with lived experience. In an ADDitude survey of nearly 2,000 women with ADHD, almost one in two respondents said that hormonal fluctuations had a “life-altering” or “severe” impact on their ADHD.

“I know that the week before my period I am a complete mess,” Addison, an ADDitude reader, said. “I have to prepare for the fact that my world feels like it’s falling apart emotionally, and I hate the way that I look the most that week. These are weeks I often avoid being with people, as I know I am not the most positive and am the most sensitive.”

“I used to have lots of irritability, food cravings, tiredness, and was fuzzy-headed three to four days before my period started,” said Connie, another reader.

“I suffer from symptoms like uncontrolled fits of anger and crying spells and feeling extremely overwhelmed the days before my period. I’m even more moody, irritable and have more trouble concentrating,” said ADDitude reader Elena.

Moreover, women with ADHD are disproportionately affected by premenstrual disorders with more than 40% of women with ADHD experiencing premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) compared to 3% to 9% of women overall.2, 3 PMDD is also heavily tied to hormonal shifts and mental health.

“PMDD is caused by a high sensitivity to fluctuations in estrogen and progesterone, as well as decreases in serotonin – hormonal changes that happen during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle,” wrote Dara Abraham, D.O. in an ADDitude article. “During the luteal phase that follows ovulation, estrogen decreases, as do dopamine, serotonin, and eventually progesterone. These changes cause painful and distressing symptoms until the menstruation begins and hormone levels rise again.”

The study also found that irregular menstrual cycles were linked to higher depression and anxiety symptom scores. The longer a girl had been having her menstrual cycles, the stronger the link between irregular periods and depression and anxiety symptoms became. Likewise, earlier age at menarche was associated with higher depression symptom scores.

While the study focused specifically on early age at menarche, previous research suggests that early puberty more broadly may have an association to ADHD.

“Researchers are examining why girls with ADHD have about twice the risk for early puberty, and why autistic girls are up to four times more likely to experience early puberty compared to other children,” wrote Molly Nikolas, Ph.D. in an ADDitude article. “In addition to higher rates of obesity and social stress, which could accelerate the onset of puberty, neurodivergent girls may experience differences in dopamine activity, stress response, and immune and neuroendocrine systems — all of which may affect sexual development.”

The researchers listed several limitations to the study. Menstrual cycle characteristics were gathered through an annual self-report, and parents reported mental health symptoms. In addition, the relationship between menstrual characteristics and mental health symptoms may be bidirectional. The researchers also reported the associations were modest and that future studies are needed to further explore the potential social and biological mechanisms involved.

The study’s authors said they hope their findings will help healthcare professionals consider menstrual cycle characteristics as potentially meaningful insight when evaluating the mental health of adolescent girls.

1 Marla, S., Gangaraju, S.H., Nguyen, J. et al. Association between menstrual cycle characteristics and mental health in early adolescence. Eur Child Adolesc Psychiatry 35, 4035–4049 (2026). https://doi.org/10.1007/s00787-026-03163-8

2 Team, A. E. (2025). PMDD and ADHD: Understanding the connection and managing symptoms. ADDA – Attention Deficit Disorder Association. https://add.org/pmdd-and-adhd/

3 Pooja Thakrar, Kalyani Bhukar, Rajat Oswal, Premenstrual dysphoric disorder: Prevalence, quality of life and disability due to illness among medical and paramedical students. Journal of Affective Disorders Reports, Volume 4, 2021, 100112, ISSN 2666-9153, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jadr.2021.100112

#9465. Best meditation apps of 2027 and how to choose the right one

You open the app store to look for a meditation app and find dozens of options promising calmer days, deeper sleep, less stress, and sharper focus. It’s hard to know where to start or which claims to believe.

Below, we cover three well-known meditation apps: Calm, Headspace, and Insight Timer. We've looked at what each one offers and named what we like about it, so you can decide which one to try.

Before we dive in, a quick note on where we’re coming from. We make Calm, and we love it. We hope you will too, but another option might suit you better.

The best meditation app for you depends on what you’re looking for. To narrow it down, ask yourself these questions:

What do you want help with? Maybe it’s stress relief, better sleep, sharper focus, or a guided start as a beginner.

How much variety do you need? Some people want an extensive library to explore, while others prefer a smaller collection built around a specific goal.

How personal do you want it to feel? You might prefer an app that tailors recommendations to your mood and goals, or one that leaves the choosing to you.

What's your budget? Compare what the free and paid tiers include, since a generous free version may be all you need.

Calm is one of the most widely used meditation apps, and it also offers sleep content, music, gentle movement sessions, and more. People use Calm at night for sleep and during the day for stress.

Content library: The app features Sleep Stories, bedtime tales read by well-known voices, alongside daily meditation programs including the flagship Daily Calm. You'll also find breathwork exercises, mindful tools, soundscapes, intro courses, and longer programs on themes like anxiety and self-kindness.

Personalization: Calm’s Check-Ins let you log your mood, sleep, and gratitude, so you can spot patterns over time. You can set reminders and follow a series of sessions to build a routine.

Standout feature: For us, it's the sleep content. Sleep Stories are the first thing we’d recommend to a friend who’s struggling with sleep.

Headspace is another widely-used meditation app, and it leans into teaching. Many sessions are organized into courses that walk you through a topic step by step.

Content library: The app features beginner courses and SOS meditations, short sessions for when stress spikes. It also has themed collections for focus and movement. For sleep, there are Sleepcasts.

Personalization: Headspace offers personalized recommendations and its AI companion, Ebb, lets you talk through how you’re feeling and suggests app content in response.

Standout feature: We like how Headspace gives beginners a clear path to follow, starting with its 10-session Basics course.

Insight Timer started as a meditation timer and grew into a large library of guided meditations, with plenty of free content and a paid tier called MemberPlus.

Content library: The app hosts a catalog of meditations, talks, and music tracks, plus a meditation timer for people who prefer to sit in silence.

Personalization: You can join teacher-led challenges to help you stay on track, and the streak feature tracks how many days in a row you’ve meditated.

Standout feature: We like how much the app offers for free. With so much available, you can try a range of teachers before paying for anything.

Calm won’t be right for everyone, but here’s why we love it. (Keep in mind that this section is our point of view, not a neutral comparison.)

The daily meditations are a great place to start. There are three to choose from, and each has its own feel:

The Daily Calm, with Tamara Levitt, leans toward gentle reflection

The Daily Jay, with Jay Shetty, draws on psychology and timeless wisdom

The Daily Trip, with Jeff Warren, suits curious meditators who like to experiment

You may click with one voice more than the others, so it’s worth trying all three to find out whether you’re a Tamara, Jay, or Jeff person. (There’s a fourth daily too, the Daily Move, a short mindful movement session — a great way to get your body ready for the day.)

We’ve also produced a lot of quick meditations over the past few years, all under five minutes. So even the busiest person, or the most skeptical first-timer, has something small to try.

Sleep is the other main reason we keep coming back. With our Sleep Stories and nighttime meditations, we’ve unlocked a delightful way to let go of the worries of the day, relax your mind and body, and allow yourself to fall (and stay) asleep easily and naturally. Our 500+ Sleep Stories include some of the world’s most celebrated and soothing voices, like Harry Styles, Cynthia Erivo, Idris Elba, Rosé, and Greta Lee. With plenty more to choose from, there’s always something fresh to help you wind down and drift off.

Then there’s how the app looks and feels. The visuals lean into calming nature—think misty forests, rain on a window, slow ocean waves—so opening the app itself sets the scene for calm. And if you just need to tune out the world for a while, our Rain on Leaves soundscape is a legit vibe.

The numbers back up the impact. More than 180 million people worldwide have downloaded Calm, and its content has been studied in peer-reviewed research. For example, in one randomized trial of 88 stressed college students, those who used Calm for eight weeks reported lower perceived stress than a wait-list group.

They may help, though the research is still young. An updated review of 45 randomized trials found improvements in anxiety and depression symptoms among people using mindfulness apps, compared with control groups. The effects were modest, and the authors note we still need larger, higher-quality studies to say how much apps help and for whom.

An app also isn’t a substitute for professional care. If you’re struggling with your mental health, it’s worth talking to a doctor, who can help you find the right support.

Related read: The science behind Calm: 27 studies and surveys

Yes, though how much is free varies a lot. Calm and Headspace each offer a limited selection of free sessions plus a free trial of their paid plans, with most of the library behind a subscription. Insight Timer works the other way around: the bulk of its catalog is free, with a paid MemberPlus tier for extras like courses and offline listening.

To choose the right meditation app, start with your main goal, whether that’s stress relief, better sleep, or a guided start as a beginner. From there, check prices and any features you care about, like offline listening or language options. Then take advantage of the free trials. Most apps offer one, and it’s a good way to see how an app fits before you pay. While you’re trying it out, sample a few different narrators. A lot of meditation comes down to the voice guiding you, and finding someone you connect with can turn the practice into something you look forward to.

Calm is worth it if you want to ease stress and anxiety, sleep better, focus when your mind wanders, or learn the basics of meditation. The app may be a helpful way to build a daily mental health habit, with support for moments from a racing mind at bedtime to a hard day at work. Whether you need quick relief in the moment or ongoing support through a life change, Calm is for you.

You can try a 7-day free trial to see how it fits your flow, and you don’t need to know which content format you prefer ahead of time.

Calm and Headspace have a lot in common. Both offer guided meditation, beginner-friendly courses, short sessions for when stress spikes, sleep content, and mindful movement. The difference is in the mix and the overall feel. On Calm, you’ll find hundreds of Sleep Stories read by well-known voices, daily meditations from a rotating cast of instructors, music, soundscapes, and Emergency Calm sessions for high-stress moments. On Headspace, you’ll find a more course-led, step-by-step approach and an AI companion called Ebb. Both offer free content and a free trial, so the best way to decide is to try each and see which feels right for you.

#9464. 100 heartfelt birthday wishes for friends, family & coworkers

Pen in hand, card open, and all you've got is “Happy birthday.” Birthday wishes should come naturally, right? But putting your feelings into words can be hard.

You want your birthday wishes to feel meaningful, but you also don’t want to sound like you pulled a random quote from a book. Nobody wants a message that comes off as too stiff or too cheesy, either. And, of course, birthday greetings for different people—whether it's your best friend, your little sister, or a work colleague—should sound different, since your relationships with them are, too.

Don’t worry, we’re here to help you say exactly what you mean without going overboard. Keep reading to find 100 birthday wishes and greetings for your friends, family, and coworkers, including short happy birthday wishes you can text or drop into a card. You’ll also get tips to make them your own.

Friends are the family you choose… or the people who accidentally become family after you’ve spent a year learning all of their deepest, darkest secrets. These are the people you know you have to create the ultimate birthday wish for. After all, they know all your most embarrassing moments and still choose to be there for you through it all.

Whether you’re celebrating someone you’ve known since high school or a newer connection that just gets you, here are 30 birthday wishes that range from soft and sentimental to chaotic and hilarious.

Read more: How to be a better friend: 7 tips to improve your relationships

“You’re the kind of person people wish they had in their lives. Lucky for me, you’re in mine.”

“I’m so grateful for the way you show up both for me and yourself. Happy birthday!”

“The world is better because you’re in it. Well, my world definitely is.”

“You make me feel comfortable being myself. Never change.”

“Hope your new year is full of breakthroughs.”

“You’re the only person who makes a simple conversation feel like therapy.”

“Thank you for comforting me when I couldn’t comfort myself.”

“You make ordinary moments feel like core memories.”

“You make life less complicated, and that’s a superpower.”

“You made me laugh on days when nothing felt funny. That’s magic.”

“You’re one of the only people I’d share my fries with. That says everything.”

“You exude main character energy all day, every day.”

“May your cake be delicious and your group texts be showering you with love.”

“Honestly, I like you more than most people like their pets.”

“You’re not aging. You’re evolving into an even more iconic version of yourself.”

“I hope your texts are spicy, your skincare on point, and your peace protected.”

“You age like fine wine… or maybe boxed wine kept in a cool, dark place. It still counts.”

“Here’s to another year of you being the funniest, kindest hot mess I know.”

“Your friendship is the best gift I’ve ever gotten. But today’s about you.”

“I’d take part in crimes for you. Not big ones… but definitely misdemeanors.”

“You are loud, weird, and perfect. Never tone it down.”

“I hope your birthday is 10% wholesome and 90% unhinged. Just like you.”

“You’ve survived every awkward phase and came out iconic. Cheers to that.”

“Thanks for being the friend who makes life less filtered and way more fun.”

“Here’s to another lap around the sun with all your chaos and charm. Sign me up.”

“I hope your day is filled with only the things you love, and none of the responsibilities.”

“To the person who always knows when I need a meme or a meltdown — love you.”

“May your birthday be as drama-free as you are.”

“I want to be just like you when I grow up.”

Your family has seen you at your Sunday morning worst, but they still care enough to invite you to dinner. Whether it’s the parent who always has an extra snack, the sibling who can roast you better than anyone else, or the cousin who stepped in when life got messy, their birthday is a great chance to show them how much they mean to you. (Learn how to build better relationships through more effective communication.)

Here’s a list of 30 messages for your family that are sincere, sweet, and sneakily sentimental.

“You’ve always been the glue. And today, you’re the glitter, too.”

“You’ve shaped my life in so many ways. I’ll never forget it.”

“I hit the jackpot being related to you.”

“Your love shows up in a million small ways for me every single day.”

“Thanks for all the little things you’ve done that have added up to the big things.”

“You’ve always had my back, even when I didn’t deserve it. Thank you.”

“You’ve always made space for me. Today’s about making space for you.”

“You’ve earned every good thing that’s come your way.”

“I hope today is filled with the same care you give to everyone else.”

“You make anywhere feel like home. That’s a rare kind of magic.”

“If I could bottle your calm and kindness, I’d sell it and retire.”

“You make me feel comfortable just by being present.”

“You are proof that love doesn’t have to be loud to be strong.”

“I don’t say it enough, but I’m lucky to call you my family.”

“May your birthday be cozy, chaos-free, and cake-forward.”

“Celebrating you today and all the versions of you I’ve loved along the way.”

“I hope today feels like home: safe, warm, and full of snacks.”

“You’ve always made people feel seen. Today, we’re turning the spotlight on you.”

“I could never put into words how much you mean to me, but I’ll try anyway.”

“Your strength isn’t just in what you do… it’s in how you love.”

“Family isn’t just blood. It’s loyalty, laughter, and doing the dishes without being asked.”

“Your advice has a permanent place in my brain… whether I follow it or not.”

“You taught me how to stand up for myself, but also how to fold a fitted sheet. Iconic.”

“Happy birthday to the one person who always knows where my stuff is.”

“You’ve survived all the family gatherings without strangling anyone. That’s growth.”

“You’re not just getting older. You’re getting more legendary.”

“Here’s to fewer group texts and more celebrations.”

“Thanks for showing me what resilience looks like, even in sweatpants.”

“You taught me to be kind and funny, but also to never microwave fish. They’re all important.”

“Your hugs fix things that even coffee can’t.”

Coworkers are special. They’ve witnessed your 9am panic spiral, your 2pm snack hunt, and your 4:45pm existential crisis all in one day.

With some, you may be close outside of work. With others, you could just be trying to make their days a little better between budget reviews. No matter how deep your connection might be, a thoughtful message goes a long way.

These birthday wishes for your coworkers strike a balance between warmth and professionalism. After all, even in the corporate world, a little sincerity never hurts. (Check out these 13 tips for effective communication at work.)

“Hope your birthday is as productive as your best Monday (minus the emails).”

“Thanks for making the workplace 80% more tolerable and 100% more human.”

“If anyone deserves cake today, it’s you (and probably a raise if we’re being real).”

“May your notifications be silenced and your coffee strong.”

“Hope your day is filled with praise, pastries, and absolutely no meetings.”

“You deserve more than birthday wishes — you deserve PTO. Lots of it.”

“Here’s to a new year of thriving… and maybe finally taking that lunch break.”

“Wishing you a year full of wins — big, small, and petty.”

“Your professionalism is only rivaled by your playlist.”

“Appreciate your eye for detail, your steady leadership, and your GIF game.”

“You’re the reason our team group chat isn’t just logistics and silence.”

“Hope your birthday present this year is inbox zero.”

“Your calm in chaos is unmatched, so I hope you have a day that’s all calm, zero chaos.”

“Thanks for bringing zero drama to the workplace.”

“I hope today brings you the same peace you somehow bring to 10-person meetings.”

“Your presence makes a difference, even if we don’t say it enough.”

“Working with you always feels like teamwork.”

“Your work matters. But more importantly, you matter.”

“If we had an office superlative for ‘Most Likely to Keep It Together,’ you’d win.”

“Hope your birthday is as smooth as your best project launch.”

“You bring balance to the madness. Don’t ever leave us.”

Not every birthday needs a full paragraph. Sometimes you just want a line you can text in ten seconds or drop into a card without it sounding canned. A short birthday wish still counts.

“Happy birthday! Hope this year is kind to you.”

“Wishing you a day full of good people, good cake, and zero nonsense.”

“Happy birthday! Hope you feel celebrated from start to finish.”

“Thinking of you today and hoping it's a good one.”

“Hope your birthday brings a little extra joy and a lot less to-do list.”

“Happy birthday! May this year throw a few good surprises your way.”

“Happy birthday to someone who makes life better for the people around them.”

“Here's to a year of good news and better company.”

“Hope your day is full of love, laughter, and one excellent dessert.”

If a plain “happy birthday” feels too bare, one extra line does the trick, like naming an inside joke or something you're glad they're around for.

The best birthday message is one that’s honest, reflecting how you feel about the person. Whether it’s a thoughtful one-liner or a whole paragraph, what matters most is that it sounds like you and is from the heart.

To start writing a thoughtful birthday wish, think about what this person brings to your life. Are they the person who makes you laugh when things get heavy? Do they show up when others flake? Start there, and be as specific as possible.

You could even include a shared memory, a personal trait you admire, or something they’ve done recently that made you proud. It doesn’t matter if it’s short or long — just that it’s real and meaningful to you.

If you don't know the person well, start your message by being warm and casual. Something like, “Wishing you a joyful day and a year filled with good things” works perfectly.

If it’s for someone you know in a professional context, try, “Hope your day is filled with appreciation and celebration — you deserve it.”

You don’t have to fake closeness, but you can absolutely show care.

This one depends on your relationship with the person. If humor is a shared language between the two of you, you absolutely can. Just pay attention to the tone.

Inside jokes, light teasing, or self-deprecating lines can be great, but if you’re unsure how your humor might be perceived, it’s safer to aim for warmth with a side of personality. Don’t try it if it starts feeling forced.

Let’s be honest. “Happy birthday” gets the job done, but it’s also one of the most basic options. If you want to switch it up, try something a little more personal or playful.

“Celebrating the fact that you exist today!”

“Another year of you being excellent. Carry on.”

“Hope today treats you like the royalty you are (with cake).”

“Wishing you all the good stuff, and no fine print.”

You can write a short, warm note that fits how well you know the person. One or two sentences is plenty.

If you’re close, an inside joke can work. If you’re not, thank them for something specific, like their help on a project or the way they greet everyone in the morning. For example, “Happy birthday, Priya. Thank you for always making time to help.”

It’s usually best to skip jokes about age or appearance, especially in a card other people will read. If a group card is going around, add your name and one line of your own instead of repeating what’s already written.

A short, sincere happy birthday message is one or two sentences that greet the person and share one kind thought. It doesn’t need a joke or a long story to mean something (and it works the same way in a text, a card, or on social media).

A basic format is the person’s name, “happy birthday,” and one line about them or your hopes for their year. For example, “Happy birthday, Maya. I’m so glad you’re in my life.” Or, “Happy birthday, Dan. Hope this year brings you more rest and more cake.”

#9463. Closing the Skills Gap for Autistic Employees

The unemployment rate for workers with autism is staggering. One Australian company is aiming to change that.

In Australia, the unemployment rate for neurodivergent adults hovers around 34%, nearly eight times the national average. Clearly, there is a stigma around hiring neurodivergent people and it stems from a fear of the unknown. One not-for-profit company, Australian Spatial Analytics (ASA), is working to fix that.

ASA was established in 2020 to increase workforce participation among young neurodivergent adults by training them in big data for the geospatial and digital engineering fields, then placing them in corporate and government sectors. At ASA, we leverage these employees’ cognitive strengths — attention to detail, pattern recognition, laser-sharp focus, and innovative problem-solving skills, all of which are invaluable in these fields.

About 80% of ASA’s staff identify as neurodivergent, which includes ADHD, autism, dyslexia, dyscalculia, and dyspraxia. ASA’s recruitment process goes beyond conventional practices; it assesses potential candidates based on transferable skills, hobbies, and interests, rather than relying on formal qualifications or previous experience. Many of the new data analysts we have successfully placed in jobs are in paid positions for the first time.

[Read: We’re Hiring – ADHD-Friendly Careers]

Yet the analysts’ value to their employers is without questions. Executives have praised the ASA-trained analysts who have joined their companies, citing their work ethic, dedication, and problem-solving skills.

During the job-seeking process, ASA provides candidates with sample interview questions 48 hours in advance to help minimize anxiety. Once hired, employees receive comprehensive and paid on-the-job training that includes soft skills like communication and self-advocacy coaching.

[Read: Nail Your Job Interview – 3 Strategies for Neurodivergent Applicants]

Based on our experience, creating a supportive and productive environment requires only minor accommodations. Flexible start and finish times, predictable routines, the option for hybrid work to reduce commuting stress, adjustable lighting, noise-canceling headphones, and direct communication make a profound difference, not only for neurodivergent people, but for everyone in the workplace.

To help change paradigms, ASA offers a Neurodiversity in the Workplace Training Program for other organizations. It covers neurodiversity awareness, plus effective strategies for communication, managing anxiety in the work environment, leading neurodiverse teams, and promoting neurodivergent inclusion.

Ultimately, our goal is to put ourselves out of business.

Karly Ischenko is a Human Resources Business Partner at Australian Spatial Analytics.

#9462. Two Everyday Drink Swaps Are Linked To Less Weight Gain

Swapping just three drinks a week was linked to less weight gain over four years. What mattered was which drinks people gave up.

Swapping just three drinks a week was linked to less weight gain over four years. What mattered was which drinks people gave up.

Swapping sugary drinks for water is linked to less weight gain over time, according to a study of more than 140,000 adults.

Replacing them with diet drinks shows much the same pattern.

Switching from diet drinks to water was linked to a much smaller difference in weight.

Both swaps could make a difference by cutting the calories people get from their usual soft drinks.

A diet version can also preserve the familiar sweet taste, which may make the change easier for some people to stick with.

The findings suggest that the drink someone gives up may matter more for their weight than which of these two alternatives they choose.

The researchers drew on three long-running US studies that followed nurses and other health professionals for a typical period of 28 years.

Participants regularly reported what they drank and how much they weighed, allowing researchers to see how their drinking habits and weight shifted over four-year periods.

The researchers estimated about 1.4 kg less weight gain over four years when three sugary drinks a week were replaced with either water or diet drinks.

The estimated difference for replacing three diet drinks a week with water was only about a tenth of a kilogram over the same period.

People who cut back on sugary drinks tended to gain less weight whether or not they increased their intake of diet drinks.

The researchers estimated the swaps from changes in people’s reported habits, so the study can show associations but cannot establish how much weight any individual would gain or lose after making the switch.

Replacing a regular soft drink with its diet version changes the calories while keeping much of the experience of having a sweet drink.

Switching to water also removes the sweet taste, which may change how much sweetness people prefer over time.

In a separate year-long randomised trial, people assigned to replace sugary drinks with unsweetened ones showed a greater drop in their preferred level of sweetness than those assigned to artificially sweetened drinks (Ebbeling et al., 2020).

That change in taste preference offers a possible reason why an unsweetened choice might become more appealing with time.

The study was published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition (Espinosa et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9461. How to spend Christmas alone (and actually enjoy it)

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

It’s Christmas morning. The street outside is still, your phone hasn’t buzzed with plans, and the whole day is wide open, with no schedule and no one to check in with. It might feel like a relief, or it might ache. Sometimes it’s both in the same hour.

Maybe you’re single, estranged or far from family, working the holiday, grieving, or just not in the mood to celebrate. But no matter why you’re spending Christmas alone, the day can still feel warm and full.

In fact, there are plenty of ways to make the day your own. Here you’ll find ideas for staying in or going out, plus what to do if it gets hard.

If you’re spending Christmas on your own, you’re far from the only one. More people live alone than ever, and plenty of people simply prefer a quiet holiday.

With that in mind, being alone and feeling lonely aren't the same thing. Being alone is a circumstance: no one else is around. Loneliness is a feeling of disconnection, and it can show up at a packed holiday table or an empty house.

So what makes time alone feel good rather than lonely? A big factor may be whether you have a say in how you spend it. In three studies where people reported on their moments throughout the day, time alone felt more positive when people chose it for themselves.

If you didn’t choose to be alone this Christmas, it’s okay if that stings. What you do with the day is still up to you.

Whether you’re in the mood for a slow day under a blanket, time out among people, or a bit of both, you don’t owe anyone an explanation for how you spend your day.

If you’d rather stay in, here are a few ways to make the day at home feel comforting.

1. Start the morning with meditation or journaling: Settle into a comfortable position and let your eyes close or soften. Tune into your breath and the sensations in your body. When thoughts about the day ahead drift in, notice them, then gently return to your breath. Journaling is another way to check in with how you’re feeling.

💙 Want some guidance for those few minutes? Settle into the Mornings meditation on Calm.

2. Cook or order the meal you really want: Skip the turkey-and-trimmings unless you love them. Go for whatever you're craving, whether that’s a roast for one, pancakes at noon, or your go-to takeout. Choosing food you’re excited about can turn an ordinary meal into a treat.

💙 Listen to Piano for Rainy Days: Nice & Cozy while you cook.

4. Do a movie marathon on your own terms: You get to choose what you watch, and no one talks through the good parts. Line up your favorite holiday films, or skip the Christmas theme entirely and binge the series you’ve been saving.

5. Get lost in a book or an audiobook: A long, quiet day is a great chance to sink into a story without interruption. If your eyes get tired, switch to an audiobook while you putter around or lie on the couch.

💙 Discover ten self-love activities to improve your well-being.

If you’d like to spend the day out of the house, these ideas include solo outings and activities around other people. Holiday hours often change and volunteer spots fill up, so check details as early as you can..

6. Spend time somewhere green: Stroll along a park path or trail, or find a bench and settle in for a while. Time in green space has been shown to quiet a busy mind. In one study, adults who walked for 90 minutes in nature reported less rumination (the looping, negative thinking that can feed low moods) than those who walked along a busy road.

💙 Ready to step outside? Try Calm’s Nature Walk meditation with Dr. Eric López to soak in the sights, sounds, and smells around you.

7. Volunteer for a few hours: Soup kitchens, shelters, and animal rescues often need extra hands on Christmas Day. Volunteering connects you with people who share a purpose, and research suggests performing acts of kindness may boost your well-being.

💙 Feeling the urge to give back? Tune into the Random Acts of Kindness meditation on Calm to see how small gestures add up.

8. Join a community meal or gathering: Many community centers and local groups host open Christmas meals. It’s a low-pressure way to share the day with others, even if only for a couple of hours.

9. Find somewhere that’s open: Movie theaters, some cafés and restaurants, and hotel lounges often keep holiday hours. Even a little time around other people, strangers included, can bring a touch of connection to your day.

10. Take a day trip: Head to a nearby town, hike a new trail, or visit a spot you’ve been meaning to see. A change of scenery can make the day feel like an occasion.

There are many ways to make a quiet day feel less lonely, from a quick text to a mindfulness practice. Choose whichever of these appeal to you.

Send a text, leave a voice note, or call someone you care about. If loved ones are far away, you could:

Schedule a call in advance, especially if you’re in different time zones.

Do an activity together over video, like cooking or watching a movie.

Ask for a family recipe, make it, and share how it turned out.

You can start a tradition on your own. Keep it small and simple, such as a letter to your future self you open next year or a movie you rewatch every December 25.

💙 Not sure where to start? Explore Redefining Traditions with therapist Kati Morton on Calm.

If you feel loneliness creeping in, a loving-kindness meditation may help you feel more connected. In one study, people who did a short loving-kindness meditation reported more feelings of social connection toward strangers than those who did a control task.

💙 Press play on the Loving-Kindness meditation on Calm.

Give yourself one thing to look forward to after your shift, such as a comfort meal or a call with someone you love. Treat yourself during the day with a good coffee or a walk on your break. You can also celebrate with others on another day, and it’s just as meaningful.

💙 If you’re still feeling lonely after the holiday, here are seven tips to deal with loneliness.

Even if you’ve chosen to be alone, Christmas can bring up emotions like sadness, envy, or grief. Here’s how to work through them.

Other people’s picture-perfect holiday photos can leave you feeling like you’re missing out. Try stepping away from your phone for a few hours. Those posts are a highlight reel, and the rest of their day rarely looks as polished.

If the feeling lingers, try self-compassion: meeting yourself with the same warmth you’d offer a friend who’s feeling down. In a review of studies, people who practiced self-compassion reported lower anxiety, depression, and stress than people who didn’t. You could tell yourself, “This is hard, but I’m doing my best, and that’s enough.”

💙 Practice being a Friend on the Inside with Jeff Warren on Calm.

If you’re missing someone this Christmas, the day can feel especially tender. You can honor them in subtle ways: cook their favorite dish, light a candle in their memory, or write them a letter. There’s no right way to grieve, so let the day be as quiet or as full as you need.

It’s okay to keep some distance from family on Christmas if you need to. Calls and replies are optional, and so is explaining your choice. You can mute the group chat for the day if that brings you some peace.

If someone asks what you’re up to, you could say, “I’m keeping it low-key this year.” Whatever comes up, mixed feelings included, you don’t have to push it aside just because it’s the holidays.

If your sadness lingers past the holiday, disrupts your sleep or appetite, or leaves you feeling hopeless, talk to a doctor or someone you trust. If you’re in the U.S. and need support right away, call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. If you’re outside the U.S., findahelpline.com lists free local services.

If you’re alone for Christmas, it can help to give the day some structure. Pick one or two things that excite you, such as a comfort meal, a long walk, or a movie, and let the rest of the day unfold naturally. A quick call or text with a loved one can be a nice touch, too.

It’s normal to want to spend Christmas alone. After a long or busy year, a quiet day can be restful, and preferring it doesn’t mean anything is wrong. Plan the day around what appeals to you.

If you’d rather not stay home on Christmas, there are plenty of places to spend the day. Look for open movie theaters, cafés, and parks nearby, or join a community meal at a local center. You could also volunteer for an organization to meet people while contributing to a cause. Holiday hours vary, so it’s worth confirming before you head out.

If you’re single on Christmas, the day is yours to spend however you want. You could cook something you love, explore a new spot, or go for a casual meal or movie with friends.

If you’re feeling sad or lonely on Christmas, let yourself feel those emotions without judgment. Consider reaching out to a loved one, even briefly. A short meditation can also bring some relief. If the sadness feels overwhelming or won’t lift, speak to a doctor or someone you trust.

It’s okay to skip Christmas altogether. You can treat December 25 as an ordinary day: rest, work, or do something unrelated to the holiday. If the season stirs up grief or stress, stepping back from holiday plans is one way to look after yourself.

A solo tradition can be anything that brings you comfort, whether that’s a special breakfast, a journal entry, or a new ornament you pick out every year. A simple tradition is more likely to stick from year to year.

"Is Social Security taxable?" is one of the most common tax questions retirees ask — and the answer frustrates almost everyone: it depends. Depending on your total income, anywhere from 0% to 85% of your Social Security benefits can be subject to federal income tax. The tax was introduced in 1983, originally affecting about 10% of recipients. Today, because the income thresholds were never indexed for inflation, roughly 56% of Social Security recipients pay tax on their benefits.

The good news: even in the worst case, you'll never pay tax on 100% of your Social Security. The bad news: the formula for calculating the taxable amount is one of the most convoluted in the entire tax code. In this guide, we'll break it down into plain English, show you exactly how to calculate what you owe, and — most importantly — share strategies the FI community uses to reduce or eliminate the tax entirely.

The IRS uses a special formula called "combined income" (also called "provisional income") to determine how much of your Social Security benefits are taxable. Here's the formula:

Combined Income = Adjusted Gross Income (AGI) + Nontaxable Interest + Half of Social Security Benefits

The resulting number determines which taxation tier you fall into. Notice that the thresholds haven't changed since 1993 — they are not adjusted for inflation, which means more retirees cross into taxable territory every year.

Important: "Up to 85% taxed" does not mean you pay an 85% tax rate. It means 85% of your benefits are added to your taxable income and taxed at your ordinary income rate. If you're in the 22% bracket and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you'd owe 22% on $25,500 — roughly $5,610.

This is the most common Social Security tax confusion. When the IRS says "up to 85% of benefits are taxable," it means 85% of your benefit amount gets added to your taxable income and taxed at your regular rate. If your marginal rate is 22% and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you owe about $5,610 — not $25,500. The effective tax rate on your full benefit in this example is about 18.7%.

Let's walk through a real example. Meet Sarah: she's 67, single, retired, and receives $24,000 per year in Social Security benefits. She also has $18,000 in IRA withdrawals and $2,000 in municipal bond interest.

Step 2: Determine the Tier Sarah is single with combined income of $32,000, which falls between $25,000 and $34,000. She's in the 50% tier — up to 50% of her benefits may be taxable.

Step 3: Calculate the Taxable Amount The actual calculation involves comparing two formulas and taking the lesser amount. For the 50% tier:

Sarah adds $3,500 to her other taxable income. At a 12% marginal rate, that's roughly $420 in additional federal tax on her Social Security.

Beyond federal taxes, 13 states also tax Social Security benefits to some degree as of 2026. Each state has its own thresholds and exemption amounts:

The remaining 37 states and Washington, D.C. do not tax Social Security benefits at all. If you're planning where to retire, this is a meaningful factor — especially if you have substantial SS benefits combined with other retirement income.

The FI community has identified several strategies that can significantly reduce the tax bite on Social Security benefits. The key insight: since taxation is based on combined income, controlling your income in retirement is the lever.

This is the single most powerful strategy. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula. If you retire early (before Social Security age), you have a window of low-income years to convert Traditional IRA/401(k) money to Roth.

Example: Between ages 55 and 67, you convert $500,000 from your Traditional IRA to a Roth — paying tax at rates as low as 10-12%. When you claim Social Security at 67, your Roth withdrawals don't push you into a higher SS taxation tier. Instead of 85% of your benefits being taxable, you might pay tax on 0-50%.

The math is dramatic over a 25+ year retirement. Converting at 12% during early retirement to avoid 22%+ taxation on Social Security for decades produces enormous tax savings.

Every dollar of AGI pushes you toward the 50% or 85% taxation tiers. Strategic levers include:

Once you reach age 70.5, you can donate up to $105,000 per year directly from your IRA to a qualified charity. This satisfies your Required Minimum Distribution (RMD) without the distribution being included in your AGI. Lower AGI means lower combined income, which means less Social Security is taxable.

For charitably inclined retirees, QCDs are one of the most tax-efficient giving strategies available — they simultaneously reduce your income tax AND reduce the tax on your Social Security benefits.

Delaying Social Security from 62 to 70 increases your benefit by roughly 77%. But there's a secondary benefit: during the delay years, you have more room to do Roth conversions at low tax rates without Social Security benefits adding to your combined income. The combination of larger benefits and lower taxation on those benefits makes delay doubly powerful for tax optimization.

If you retire before claiming Social Security, you have a golden window for Roth conversions. With little or no earned income and no SS benefits, you can convert Traditional IRA money to Roth at the lowest tax brackets of your lifetime. Every dollar you convert is a dollar that will never increase the tax on your Social Security benefits. This window closes permanently once you start claiming.

A step-by-step walkthrough for estimating what you owe.

List your AGI from all sources: IRA/401(k) withdrawals, pension income, wages, dividends, capital gains, rental income. Get your total Social Security benefit from your SSA-1099 form.

Pro tip: Don't forget nontaxable municipal bond interest — it counts in the combined income formula even though it's not on your 1040.

Add your AGI + nontaxable interest + half of your Social Security benefits. This "combined income" number determines your taxation tier.

Compare your combined income to the thresholds: Single — $25K (50% tier), $34K (85% tier). Married filing jointly — $32K (50% tier), $44K (85% tier).

For the 50% tier: take 50% of combined income above the lower threshold (capped at 50% of benefits). For the 85% tier: the calculation is more complex — use IRS Publication 915 worksheet or tax software.

Pro tip: Tax software handles this automatically. If doing it by hand, IRS Publication 915 has the complete worksheet.

The taxable portion of your Social Security gets added to your other taxable income and taxed at your marginal rate. Check if your state also taxes Social Security.

For single filers, Social Security becomes partially taxable when combined income exceeds $25,000 (50% tier) and up to 85% taxable above $34,000. For married filing jointly, the thresholds are $32,000 (50% tier) and $44,000 (85% tier). These thresholds have not changed since 1993 and are not indexed for inflation.

No. Social Security benefits are not earned income. They are classified as unearned income for tax purposes. This distinction matters for things like the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), IRA contribution eligibility, and the Social Security earnings test (which only applies to earned income like wages and self-employment).

No — and this is why Roth accounts are so powerful in retirement. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula used to determine Social Security taxation. Converting Traditional IRA money to Roth before claiming Social Security can dramatically reduce the tax on your benefits for life.

Yes. File Form W-4V with the Social Security Administration to have federal income tax withheld from your benefits. You can choose 7%, 10%, 12%, or 22% withholding. This avoids the surprise of a large tax bill at filing time. State tax withholding varies by state.

Social Security benefits are included in the Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) calculation that determines Medicare Part B and Part D premium surcharges (IRMAA). High-income retirees can pay significantly more for Medicare — up to 3.4 times the standard premium. Managing MAGI in retirement affects both Social Security taxation and Medicare costs.

There have been numerous proposals to reform Social Security taxation, including indexing the thresholds for inflation, raising the taxable percentage above 85%, or eliminating the tax entirely. As of 2026, no changes have been enacted. The thresholds have remained unchanged since 1993, meaning inflation automatically pushes more retirees into taxable territory each year.

Yes, Social Security benefits can be taxable — up to 85% of your benefits may be added to your taxable income depending on your combined income. The thresholds are low ($25,000 single, $32,000 married) and haven't been adjusted for inflation since 1993, catching more retirees every year. The single most powerful strategy is Roth conversions during early retirement years before claiming Social Security. Every dollar in a Roth account is a dollar that won't push your Social Security into the taxable zone. Plan your retirement income sources deliberately, and you can reduce or eliminate this tax entirely.

#9459. Half of People with Eating Disorders Show Signs of Undiagnosed ADHD: Study

More than 50% of people receiving treatment for eating disorders, especially bulimia and binge-eating, may have ADHD, though few are diagnosed, according to a new study.

Roughly half of adults in treatment for eating disorders display symptoms of ADHD, though few are diagnosed, according to a new cross-sectional study published in Journal of Eating Disorders.1

The study, conducted at Esquirol Hospital in Limoges, France, included 120 participants, 95.8% of whom were female. Using the ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS v1.1), researchers screened participants for ADHD, then followed up to confirm the screening with the Diagnostic Interview for ADHD (DIVA 2.0). More than half (61) of the participants met criteria for ADHD, according to these measures, though only two had received a prior diagnosis. Bulimia nervosa and binge-eating disorder were more strongly associated with ADHD than was anorexia nervosa.

Participants who showed symptoms of ADHD also had more psychiatric comorbidities and higher rates of impulsivity, body dissatisfaction, and smoking and alcohol use. Personality assessments revealed that participants with ADHD symptoms showed greater dependence on rewards, while those who did not exhibited higher rates of self-regulation.

“These findings support ADHD screening and integrated treatments targeting impulsivity and attentional dysregulation,” wrote the study’s authors.

In “ADHD and Eating Disorders: Research, Diagnosis & Treatment Guidelines,” Roberto Olivardia, Ph.D., explores the myriad biological and genetic factors that may predispose individuals with ADHD to eating disorders. They include:

Further research is needed to understand all possible mechanisms, as well as the benefit of ADHD treatment on eating disorder recovery.

In an ADDitude guest blog post titled, “Dopamine, Not Discipline: The ADHD–Eating Disorder Link I Was Missing,” Penelope Mazzetti offers these insights: “My ‘out-of-control eating’ wasn’t an issue of willpower; it was partly sensory-seeking behavior, a well-documented ADHD trait. As ADHD brains like mine are chronically low in dopamine, we are wired to seek stimulation, and food just happens to be fast, legal, and always available.”

1Bonilla, A., Torelli, S., Virevialle, AL. et al. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in adults with eating disorders: prevalence, clinical correlates, and personality profiles. J Eat Disord (2026). https://doi.org/10.1186/s40337-026-01793-6

#9457. Psychiatry ICD-10 Codes

This is a comprehensive table of psychiatry ICD 10 codes used by researchers and healthcare professionals and personnel – nurses, medical coders, physicians, et al. This table has been curated for psychiatrists and mental health specialists to include all psychiatry ICD 10 codes and classifications relevant to psychiatric and mental health conditions.

The World Health Organization originally authorized the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD-10) for mortality coding and classification from United States death certificates. A Clinical Modification (ICD-10-CM) was developed for medical diagnoses, and a Procedure Coding System (ICD-10-PCS) was used to classify inpatient procedures. Psychiatry ICD-10 codes in the ICD-10-CM and ICD-10-PCS replace and update psychiatry ICD codes in all three volumes of the ICD-9-CM.

#9456. Panic attack hangover: 12 ways to recover and feel better

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

You’re finally on the other side of the panic attack. The chest tightness has eased, the shaking has stopped, and your breathing feels more steady. But instead of relief, there’s a strange exhaustion settling in, like you just ran a marathon you don’t remember signing up for. This is often called a panic attack hangover.

The hours (or even days) after a panic episode can feel foggy and disorienting. You might experience headaches, sore muscles, difficulty concentrating, or an overwhelming need to crash. These symptoms can feel alarming if no one ever mentioned they might show up, but they’re actually a normal part of the body’s recovery process.

Understanding what’s happening can ease some of the worry, and having a few gentle tools on hand can make the aftermath feel a little less isolating. Here’s what to know about panic attack hangovers, along with research-backed tips to support yourself through them.

A panic attack hangover is the period of lingering after-effects that follow a panic attack. Even though the rush of fear and physical symptoms has eased, your body can still feel off-balance for hours or even days afterward. Many people describe it as feeling strangely similar to an alcohol hangover: foggy, heavy, and emotionally sensitive.

The experience can be unsettling, especially if you didn’t expect panic to have an “aftermath.” But panic attack hangovers are both common and temporary. They’re simply your body’s way of recovering from an intense stress response.

Note: This guide focuses on panic attacks. If you’ve had an anxiety attack, which builds more gradually, read How to manage symptoms and find ease after an anxiety attack instead.

While panic attack hangovers can happen at any time, the effects aren’t the same for everyone. Still, there are some common symptoms people notice after a panic attack, some more frequently than others.

Fatigue or exhaustion: You might feel like your body’s battery has been completely drained.

Brain fog: You could find it hard to focus, remember things, or think clearly.

Muscle tension or soreness: Your jaw, shoulders, or chest might feel tight, achy, or tender from holding too much stress.

Emotional sensitivity: You may notice yourself crying more easily or feeling unusually fragile in everyday situations.

Headaches: You might experience pressure or pain often triggered by stress, shallow breathing, or unconscious clenching.

Digestive issues: You could have nausea, stomach discomfort, or sudden changes in your appetite that don’t seem to track.

Sleepiness or difficulty sleeping: You may find yourself crashing hard into deep rest or lying awake because you’re unable to settle down.

These symptoms usually fade within a day, although they can last longer depending on the amount of sleep you get, your stress levels, and your overall health. If they’re frequent or overwhelming, though, it may be a sign to get additional support.

The reason panic leaves a hangover comes down to how your body handles stress. A panic attack sends your nervous system into full alert: your heart races, your breath quickens, and your muscles tighten. This is an ancient survival mechanism that’s been designed to keep you safe in an emergency.

The problem? Even when the threat isn’t real, your body still goes through the motions without an outlet to use up that surge of energy.

Once the attack ends, your system shifts into recovery mode. That crash can leave you feeling shaky, sore, and depleted… much like finishing an intense workout. On top of that, the emotional weight of the experience—fear, vulnerability, or the worry it might happen again—can keep your brain buzzing even while your body’s trying to rest.

This combination of physical exhaustion and emotional strain creates the foggy, heavy state that many people call a panic attack hangover.

Related read: Panic attack vs. anxiety attack? Here's the difference

Panic attack hangovers can hit you hard, and you may not have the energy to do much after. These ideas are simple, low-lift, and designed for the days when everything feels like just too much.

Pick what’s doable today and ignore the rest: your nervous system will get the memo.

Your body just ran an internal marathon, and it’s important to be kind to it. If you can, postpone non-urgent tasks and try to give yourself a small recovery window.

Set a 10–15 minute timer, lie down or sit with support behind your back, and let your eyes rest. If you’re at work, try a short break, plus two minutes of slow breathing in a quiet corner. A pause can often help you recover faster.

Related read: Stressed and short on time? Here's how to try micro-meditation

Staying hydrated and keeping your blood sugar steady can help you feel more balanced as your body recovers from a panic attack. Dehydration and dips in blood sugar can make fatigue, headaches, and brain fog worse.

Drink water or an electrolyte beverage and have a simple snack, like fruit with nut butter, yogurt, or toast. This helps give your system some fuel to reset.

Slow, gentle breathing tells your nervous system that you’re safe. Try this for 2–3 minutes: Inhale through your nose for four counts, and then exhale through pursed lips for six or eight.

Longer exhales can help your nervous system shift from fight-or-flight into rest-and-digest mode. But only do this if you feel comfortable. Don’t try to force anything.

💙 If you need some guidance, check out Reset with the Breath with Jay Shetty on the Calm app.

Panic can cause you to tighten your muscles, especially in the jaw, chest, shoulders, and hands. Short, light movements help clear it all without overexertion.

You don’t have to do anything too intense. Simple shoulder rolls, gentle neck circles, a slow doorframe chest stretch, or a five-minute walk around the block or office floor can all help. If you’re seated, simply unclench your jaw, open and close your hands 10 times, or shake out your arms. The point is to loosen everything up.

💙 Need a little extra support? Try the Softening Anxiety Daily Move session with Mel Mah on the Calm app.

Quick temperature shifts, like splashing cool water on your face or holding something cold, can help ground you and interrupt the leftover jitters after a panic attack.

This is because it’s actually a form of grounding that allows your nervous system to anchor itself back to the present moment.

Related read: 18 grounding techniques to help relieve anxiety

Decision fatigue amplifies the brain fog that comes after a panic attack, so try to cut down on the number of choices you’re making.

Trim your to-do list to one or two essentials, and choose “good enough” over perfect. Reheat leftovers instead of cooking, tell your coworkers you’re running a little behind, and move all noncritical tasks to the next day. It sounds simple, but having that space will help more than you know.

Reduce stimulation to ease the post-panic attack stress. Dim overhead lights, switch to warm lamps, lower the volume on any music or background noise, and silence non-urgent notifications on your phone and laptop for an hour.

If noise is unavoidable, try earplugs or a brown-noise playlist. If you enjoy aromatherapy a familiar scent (like lavender, vanilla, or eucalyptus) can also be grounding.

Writing a few lines about your feelings and symptoms post-panic attack can help your brain process what happened and move forward. Research shows that journaling supports emotional regulation, which is why so many people find it useful for panic recovery, too — even if it’s just a quick note or voice memo.

Consider reflecting on what triggered your attack, what symptoms you noticed, what helped calm you down, and what you could do differently next time. This can help give you more effective coping tools for future attacks.

Reaching out, even with a simple text, helps calm the nervous system. Social support is one of the strongest buffers for stress recovery.

Send a text to someone you trust, simply asking to check in. If talking feels like too much, having someone just sit with you can also be helpful.

Related read: How to help someone having a panic attack (and what to avoid)

After a panic attack, your system is more sensitive. Consider skipping or reducing how much caffeine you drink, as it can re-spark jitters. And avoid alcohol, as it’s been known to disrupt sleep and mood. Swap in decaf, herbal tea, or a half-caf and make sure to focus on nutrition and hydration to help support recovery.

Fatigue after a panic attack is real, and quality sleep helps reset your stress response. Keep bedtime predictable with a wind-down routine you enjoy, darken the room, and cool it slightly.

If you desperately need a nap, cap it at 20–30 minutes, and avoid late-evening naps in order to protect nighttime sleep. If your mind spins when it’s time to go to bed, try a quiet meditation or body scan. This can help quiet the mind long enough to help you drift off faster.

💙 Fall asleep with ease thanks to the White Noise soundscape on the Calm app.

Even just knowing what you’ll do next time can take the edge off that heavy, shaky feeling that lingers after a panic attack. One simple idea? Make a three-step plan that you keep on your phone or in your wallet.

Spend two minutes on long exhales or humming.

Splash cold water on your face or run cool water over your wrists.

It also helps to add one contact you trust to call or text.

While you may not be able to prevent every spiral, it always helps to have something in your back pocket (literally) that helps you feel less alone and more ready.

Yes, a hangover can sometimes trigger panic attacks. This is because alcohol disrupts sleep, dehydrates your body, and causes blood sugar swings — and all of these effects can make your nervous system more sensitive the next day.

Alcohol also interferes with the neurotransmitters that regulate your mood, which can amplify feelings of unease or dread. If you’re already prone to anxiety, that extra stress can tip into panic.

Every person who drinks won’t necessarily have a panic attack, but if you notice a pattern between hangovers and panic, it may help to cut back, hydrate more intentionally, or avoid drinking on nights before demanding days.

For most people, the hungover feeling eases within a few hours, but it’s not unusual for fatigue or brain fog to stretch into the next day. The duration of a panic attack hangover depends on several factors: how intense the panic attack was, how long it lasted, how well you slept, and what kind of support you gave your body afterward.

Try to find the recovery plan that works best for you: getting enough water, food, gentle movement, and rest can speed up the reset. However, if you find that your hangover lasts longer than 24 hours or happens every time you panic, it may be a sign that your nervous system is under strain. In this case, getting some professional support can help.

Brain fog and fatigue are your nervous system’s way of asking for recovery time, so supporting your body can make the fog lift faster. Start with water or an electrolyte drink, followed by a small, balanced meal or snack. Light movement like walking or stretching also helps by boosting circulation and clearing leftover stress hormones, while short breaks from screens give your brain a reset.

Some people find that changing environments—stepping outside for fresh air, moving to a quieter space, or dimming harsh lighting—makes a noticeable difference in clarity. Rest is important, too, but you don’t want to overdo it. A short nap capped at 20–30 minutes usually helps more than staying in bed for hours.

The exhaustion you feel after a panic attack is the crash that comes after an adrenaline surge. Basically, when you panic, your body burns through enormous amounts of energy in a short time. Your heart rate rises, your muscles tense, and your brain goes into overdrive to scan for danger.

Even though there isn’t an actual threat, your body doesn’t know that, so it uses up its resources as if there is. Once the panic attack passes, your hormones shift, and your body needs to come down from the emotional intensity. While it’s easy to look at this exhaustion as weakness, it’s really just your body’s way of recovering from an all-systems-on alert. That’s why gentleness is key for recovery.

You can’t always prevent panic attacks, but you can definitely soften the after-effects. The most helpful strategies are proactive, or preventing one before it comes on. Think: getting consistent sleep, eating balanced meals to keep blood sugar steady, staying hydrated, and limiting alcohol or excessive caffeine.

Some people find it useful to have a short aftercare routine ready, too, such as hydrating, stretching, or texting a friend once the panic subsides. This helps to prevent the hangover from stretching out longer than necessary.

Over time, therapy and skills training can also reduce both the frequency of panic attacks and the severity of hangovers. You’ll essentially learn how to give your nervous system a softer landing.

Headaches and sore muscles are common after a panic attack. During panic, your jaw, neck, shoulders, and chest may tighten without you noticing, and fast, shallow breathing could add to the headache.

Unclenching your jaw, rolling your shoulders, or holding a cool compress to your forehead may help. Get care right away if you have a sudden, severe headache, chest pain, numbness or weakness, trouble speaking, or vision changes. If your headache lasts longer than you’d expect, check in with your doctor or primary care provider.

After a panic attack, give your body a few minutes to settle before you do anything else. Stay where you are if it’s safe, and take a few slow breaths with a longer exhale.

Shakiness or fog is a normal part of coming down from panic, so you don’t need to push through it. Once the first wave passes, tell someone you trust what happened and lower the demands on yourself for the rest of the day. The 12 tips above have ideas for the hours that follow. If panic attacks keep happening, talking with a doctor or mental health professional may help.
