#9418. When is World Meditation Day? Plus, 5 ways to celebrate

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA

So many of us live with jam-packed daily schedules, constantly juggling our responsibilities to work, family, and friends. The never-ending to-do lists can wear us down, and any remaining free time we may have is spent zoning out in front of the TV or scrolling on our phones. Taking time to pause, breathe, and connect with ourselves may feel impossible, so sometimes we need an extra push.

World Meditation Day, a day dedicated to uplifting the power of meditation and promoting regular acts of self-care, is the perfect opportunity to shift your focus back onto your mental well-being by prioritizing meditation and connecting with yourself through the hustle and bustle of everyday life.

World Meditation Day is held each year on December 21. It’s dedicated to the practice of meditation, a technique that’s been used for centuries to nurture a sense of calm and inner peace. The day is designed to promote awareness about the benefits of meditation and encourage people to bring the practice into their daily lives to restore a sense of balance and clarity.

Originating in India around 1500 B.C., meditation initially combined spirituality with the religious and philosophical life of Hindu and Buddhist traditions. The aim was to cultivate mindfulness and a deep, inward connection to the divine — or the inner self.

Meditation practices spread across Asia and to the Western world, where techniques were adapted to make them relevant to the unique spiritual, therapeutic, and practical needs of each culture.

During World Meditation Day on December 21, people around the world acknowledge and celebrate the rich history and evolution of meditation. The day reminds us of meditation's ancient roots and its wide-ranging health and well-being benefits.

In December 2024, meditation got its own spot on the global calendar when the United Nations General Assembly adopted a resolution proclaiming December 21 as World Meditation Day. The resolution invites people everywhere to observe the day in a way that suits them and to help raise awareness of the benefits of meditation.

Despite a long history, meditation is becoming more and more important in the modern world.

Stress reduction: Regular meditation may help decrease our level of stress hormones, like cortisol, helping to reduce stress and leading to improved mental health and decreased risk of stress-related diseases.

Enhanced concentration: Meditation can help train the brain to focus for longer periods, which can enhance productivity at work. This improved attention span can be extremely beneficial when we’re constantly bombarded with distractions and information.

Promotion of overall well-being: Meditation has been linked with many physical health benefits, including lowered blood pressure, reduced anxiety, and better immune system response.

Contribution to global harmony: By cultivating personal peace and mindfulness, meditation can encourage positive interactions. In this way, World Meditation Day helps promote unity across different cultures and communities.

Whether you’re an experienced meditator or new to the practice, taking part in World Meditation Day can be a fulfilling, enriching experience.

Many organizations host global meditation sessions on World Meditation Day. Connect with thousands of others around the world who are practicing meditation. This can be a powerful experience, emphasizing the unity and collective energy of the human experience.

Seek out workshops, either in-person or online, which can expose you to different meditation techniques and enhance your personal practice.

Plan or attend a group meditation session at a local park, community center, or virtually. Group meditations can help build a sense of community and shared purpose, making the practice more enjoyable and impactful.

If you prefer solitude, dedicate specific time on World Meditation Day for your personal meditation practice. Create a special session where you focus on your intentions, gratitude, or personal peace, allowing you to connect with yourself on a deeper level.

It’s always nice to share the positives in life, so why not spread the love by sharing your meditation experience on social media? Use the hashtag #WorldMeditationDay to join the trend. This can help spread awareness about the day and encourage others to get involved.

Here are a few ways you can enhance and deepen your own meditation practice in honor of World Meditation Day.

If you’re new to meditation or prefer a structured approach, guided meditations can be helpful. An experienced practitioner directs you through spoken instructions, often accompanied by calming music or natural sounds. Try a guided meditation to help you focus, explore different techniques, or maintain meditation discipline.

💙 Add the Daily Calm to your meditation routine, for a new 10-minute guided meditation each day.

Establishing a specific area in your home for meditation can significantly improve the quality of your practice and be a reminder to pause and reconnect with yourself. Make your space quiet, comfortable, and free from distractions. You can even personalize it with items that promote relaxation and peace such as cushions, candles, incense, or soothing artwork.

Explore different styles of meditation to help keep your practice fresh and engaging. Beyond the commonly known mindfulness and transcendental meditation, you might try types like zen, vipassana, or heart-centered meditation, which offer their own benefits.

💙 Dive into Practices: Meditation for Beginners, a 7-day guided meditation series, to expand your practice.

Meditation doesn't always have to be a separate part of your day. Add mindfulness techniques into daily activities like walking, eating, or even during breaks at work to help you stay present throughout the day.

💙 Explore how meditation can be practiced during your 9-5 with the Mindfulness at Work series.

Engaging with fellow meditators can provide support, motivation, and deeper insight into your practice. Look for online forums and local groups that offer meetings, discussions, and shared meditation sessions, which can be particularly enriching.

💙 Join the Daily Calm Community on Facebook to engage with other meditators and share questions and experiences from your practice.

While meditation has been around for centuries, the origin of World Meditation Day isn’t clear. World Meditation Day has been observed for many years and has grown in popularity across the globe in recent years as more people have embraced the practices and recognized their benefits.

We celebrate World Meditation Day to recognize and promote the many benefits of meditation. These benefits can include reducing stress, improving concentration, enhancing emotional health, and building a sense of peace and community. The day encourages new and seasoned meditators to dedicate time to their meditation practices and to positively impact personal and global well-being.

If you’re organizing a meditation event in your community, a few simple steps can help make your event a success.

Start by choosing a suitable location such as a community center, park, or an online platform.

Next, decide on the format of the event — for example, a guided meditation, silent meditation, or a workshop with a knowledgeable instructor.

Promote the event through local community boards, social media, and word of mouth.

Provide clear instructions about what participants should bring (such as mats or cushions) and what they should expect from the event.

There are many virtual meditation resources available to help guide your practice. Explore Calm’s variety of guided meditations, which are suitable for all sorts of different levels and goals, such as stress reduction, better sleep, or increased focus. There’s even a handy beginner series to help you get started, and blog posts on how to meditate if you need a few tips. These resources can make it easy to bring meditation into your daily routine, no matter where in the world you are or how experienced you are.

#9416. Do you work from home? Here's how to stay focused (and sane)

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Your commute is a 10-step walk from your bedroom to your desk. The coffee's freshly brewed, and you’re still in your pajama pants. For many people, these types of comforts are the benefit of working from home.

But working from home can also bring up challenges that add up over time, such as a lack of boundaries between work and rest and days that feel lonely. Luckily, the habits you build around your workday can help ease both.

Ahead, we’ll cover how to stay focused and connected while working from home, whether you went remote last month or years ago.

Working from home has upsides and downsides, and you may notice both in the same week. On the plus side:

Time and energy back: Without a commute, you may have more time and energy for the rest of your day.

Higher productivity: In a randomized study, employees who worked from home performed about 13% better than those in the office.

Flexibility without a career cost: In a follow-up study, employees who worked from home two days a week performed as well as their in-office coworkers and were promoted as often. They were also less likely to quit.

Risk of isolation: In a large 2026 study in Science, remote work was linked to about a third of the rise in isolation and mental distress.

Blurred boundaries: Without a commute or an office door, your workday can stretch into evenings and weekends.

Higher burnout rates: In a review of 44 studies from the pandemic years, remote workers often reported burnout.

Small changes to your setup can help you get into work mode. Whether you’re building your first home workspace or refreshing one you’ve used for years, these tweaks can make your workday feel smoother.

A dedicated spot: Pick one place to work, such as the corner of a room or one end of the table. Your brain may start to associate that spot with work.

Natural light: Set up near a window if you can. Morning daylight may help you feel alert during the day and sleep better at night. If you don’t have a window, a warm desk lamp paired with a bright overhead light may ease eye strain.

Physical comfort: Choose a supportive seat and raise your screen to eye level, so discomfort doesn’t pull your attention away. A cushion behind your lower back or a firm pillow under you can stand in for a special chair. If sitting for long stretches is hard on your body, switch positions throughout the day or ask your doctor about seating options that fit your needs.

Fewer distractions: Clear your work surface of anything you don’t need for the task at hand. Close extra browser tabs and silence phone notifications, since digital clutter may pull at your focus in the same way physical clutter does.

Sounds for focus: Some people work best in silence, while others prefer instrumental music or ambient sound in the background. In a noisy home, headphones or earplugs can muffle the commotion. If those don’t work for you, a closed door or a “focus time” sign can let the people you live with know you’re concentrating.

💙 Explore how lo-fi music can support your focus.

Working from home takes away some of the structure an office provides, but a solid routine can bring a bit of it back. Here are a few ideas worth trying:

A morning anchor: Pick one or two consistent habits for the first hour of your day, like making coffee or journaling. A familiar rhythm can help you feel grounded before the day’s demands roll in.

A work-mode transition: Without a commute, there’s often little time between rolling out of bed and starting work. Mark the start of your workday with a quick ritual, such as changing out of your loungewear.

Protected focus time: Block a window in your day for your most demanding tasks, ideally when your energy tends to be highest. Share those hours with anyone you live with, so they know when to give you space.

Movement breaks: At home, your day may include less movement than in an office. Use your breaks to stretch or take a short walk.

A clear finish: Set a consistent end time for your workday, and follow it when you can. Mark it with a small closing ritual, like shutting your laptop and tidying your space, so work doesn’t creep into your evening and wear you down.

💙 Build a focus routine that sticks with Calm’s 7 Days of Focus series.

The strain of working from home can sneak up on you, so it helps to have habits that support your well-being along the way. Here are five gentle tips to start.

Small, regular contact tends to help with isolation more than the occasional big effort. Put one social plan on your calendar the way you would a meeting, such as a standing coffee chat with a colleague or a coworking session. On busier days, or if you work on your own, a midday text or a voice note to a friend counts too.

💙 Want more ideas for staying connected? Here’s how to make and keep friends as an adult.

Protect your time away from work. That means no email in bed, whether it’s first thing in the morning or right before sleep. Mute work apps in the evening and tell your team when you’re offline, so no one expects a reply during that time. If your job needs you to stay reachable after hours, allow only urgent messages through.

💙 Wind down from your workday with End of the Day: Leaving Work on Calm.

Step away from your screen to eat, even for a few minutes. If your energy dips, sit near a window or head outside for some fresh air.

A short meditation or a few minutes of breathwork may be a quick way to ease stress.

a focus meditation at the start of your workday

💙 Try Calm’s three-minute Body Scan for a short guided practice.

Every so often, take a moment to check in on your mood and sleep.

feeling flat, even about work you usually enjoy

pulling away from people you normally talk to

If these linger for weeks, consider reaching out to a doctor or mental health professional. Some employers offer free counseling through an employee assistance program. If you’re self-employed, a primary care provider can refer you to options.

Low motivation while working from home is often tied to missing structure. Without coworkers nearby or a set schedule, you may miss the built-in cues an office provides, such as a colleague stopping by your desk to check in. Try building a light routine and dividing work into smaller tasks.

If you don’t have much space, start with one dedicated spot for work, even if it’s just one end of a table. Add decent lighting and a supportive seat, then store your work gear away at the end of the day so the space can feel like yours again.

If you’re a remote worker, you can start a morning routine with one or two small anchor habits before work begins. That could be a gentle stretch or a few pages of a book. Keep it short, and give yourself time to adjust.

It’s normal to feel lonely when you work from home. If you feel disconnected, contact with friends or colleagues may help, even if it’s a quick call or message.

To lower your risk of burnout, aim to set firm boundaries between work and rest. Choose an end time for your work day and take regular breaks. Those limits can help keep your work from spilling into evenings and weekends.

The best way to stay focused over a long day is to work in blocks and take pauses between them. Work on your most demanding tasks when your energy is highest, reduce visible distractions, and listen to instrumental music or ambient sound if it helps you concentrate.

Meditation may ease stress, but evidence that it improves work performance is still limited. Some studies on workplace mindfulness programs suggest they may reduce burnout and improve well-being. Effects on productivity were smaller and less certain. Most of the studies followed people for about three months or less, so less is known about long-term effects.

#9415. Van Gogh painting sells for record $190m at Sotheby’s following Nazi loot claims

Auctioneer Oliver Barker selling Blossoming Chestnut Trees on Wednesday, 18 November Courtesy Sotheby's

One of Vincent van Gogh’s last paintings, long hidden from public view, sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees) at Sotheby’s New York on Wednesday (18 November), breaking the artist’s auction record. The result helped propel two back-to-back sales to a combined $663.26m ($777.8m with fees), with additional auction records for Mary Cassatt and Aaron Douglas.

But the landmark results were high points for an evening of uneven bidding, with just more than one-third of works selling for below their pre-sale estimates. The Blaquier-Arrieta collection, billed as the most valuable collection to come to auction in New York this season, brought in $358m ($412m with fees), falling short of its roughly $450m estimate. Sotheby’s Modern Evening sale, which followed immediately afterwards, generated another $305.21m ($365.8m with fees) against a $260.2m to $378.4m overall estimate.

Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890), the most valuable lot offered across New York’s auction houses this season, had attracted attention even before reaching the rostrum. One of Van Gogh’s final paintings before his death in 1890, the work had for decades been out of public view in the Blaquier-Arrieta collection, built by Argentine sugar industry heiress Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier and her husband, Carlos Pedro Blaquier, who served as president of Argentina’s largest sugar producer. Just a day before the sale, Sotheby’s announced that a settlement had been reached between the Blaquier heirs and the heirs of the painting’s previous owners, Hedwig and Samuel Fischer, following questions about the work’s Nazi-era provenance.

Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890) sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees). Courtesy Sotheby's

Estimated to fetch around $180m, the painting hammered at $165m ($190.4m with fees) after nearly five minutes of bidding, eventually going to a bidder in the room—William Acquavella, the head of Acquavella Galleries. Despite the hammer price falling short of its estimate, the Sotheby’s-guaranteed work surpassed Van Gogh’s previous auction record of $117m with fees, set in 2022 when Orchard with Cypresses (1888) sold at Christie’s Paul Allen sale. The result also made it the second most valuable object ever sold at Sotheby’s, behind Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914–16), which fetched $236.4m with fees during last November’s marquee sales, and the fourth most valuable painting ever sold at auction.

Soon afterwards, Paul Cézanne’s Arlequin (1888-90) came to the rostrum. The painting, the last of the artist’s four works from the series still in public hands, hammered at $99m ($111m with fees), falling short of its $120m estimate. It also failed to surpass Cézanne’s auction record, set during the same 2022 Paul Allen sale at Christie’s New York, when the landscape La Montagne Sainte-Victoire (1888-90) fetched $138m with fees. Nevertheless, Arlequin became the most valuable Cézanne painting from the Harlequin series to sell at auction.

Ultimately, six of the collection’s 12 lots hammered below their low estimates, while five sold within or at their estimate ranges. Just one work exceeded expectations: the final lot, Camille Pissarro’s Maison de Piette à Montfoucault, effet de neige, avec un homme portant un fagot (1875), which hammered at $1.62m ($2m with fees), against a $700,000 to $900,000 estimate.

The subsequent Modern Evening sale generated $305.21m ($365.8m with fees), although bidding was similarly patchy. Of the works sold, 14 hammered below their low estimates, 21 sold within their estimate ranges and 11 exceeded their high estimates.

The top lot was René Magritte’s L’Ami de l’ordre (1964), which hammered at $39m ($45.5m with fees), far surpassing its $25m to $35m estimate. Combining the artist’s signature bowler-hatted figure with a nighttime landscape, the painting was consigned by the estate of beauty pioneer Sydell Miller. Two years ago, 25 works from her collection brought in $215.9m with fees during a single-owner auction at Sotheby’s November marquee sales. According to Sotheby’s, only one related composition now remains in private hands. L’Ami de l’ordre is the most valuable Magritte painting featuring a bowler hat to sell at auction.

Harriet Tubman (1931) by Aaron Douglas. Courtesy Sotheby's

One of the evening’s most exciting results came courtesy of the Harlem Renaissance artist Aaron Douglas, whose Harriet Tubman (1931) shattered his previous auction record. The painting depicts the American abolitionist with her arms raised overhead, breaking a chain amid a leafy landscape and a smoking cannon. Estimated at $2.5m to $3.5m, it hammered at $12m ($14.48m with fees) after a seven-minute bidding battle. At one point, the competition pitted father and daughter against each other on the telephones, bidding on behalf of their respective clients: George Wachter, Sotheby’s chairman of the Americas, and Jacqueline Wachter, vice-chairman of private sales for contemporary art and head of the Los Angeles office. The result far surpassed Douglas’s previous auction record of $600,000, set at Swann in 2008. Proceeds from the sale will benefit Bennett College, one of just two historically Black women’s colleges in the US.

Mary Cassatt also established a new auction record when Summertime (1894–95) hammered at $11m ($13.3m with fees) to an online bidder, exceeding its $7m to $10m estimate. The result surpassed her previous record of $7.49m, set at Christie’s New York in 2022. The painting came from the collection of the late oil tycoon Armand Hammer, with proceeds benefiting his eponymous foundation.

Only one lot failed to sell: Remedios Varo’s El vagabundo, which passed at $1.5m. Three other works, by Henri Matisse, Cézanne and Magritte, were withdrawn during the sale. Together, the withdrawn lots carried estimates totalling between $12.5m and $18.5m.

#9414. What Does Gen Z Think About Political Polarization?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Polarization is a fact of political life in the U.S. today. Gen Z, however, is less inclined than older generations to view it as a permanent fixture in American politics, according to research by students in the Stanford political science course Democracy in the Balance: Polarization and the Road Ahead. Students found that Gen Z is more optimistic than any other age group about the possibility of bridging the political divide in America.

“Polarization doesn’t seem to be a fixed trend in Gen Z’s minds,” said Jadon Urogdy. “We have a bright future. Our identities and views are still malleable, and that’s exactly why this moment matters so much.”

Urogdy and his classmates also found that Gen Z, which is the cohort born between 1997 and 2012 and considered the first true “digital natives,” is more comfortable than their elders in having a political conversation online—findings that suggest they may be more reachable and receptive to online interventions aimed at reducing polarization.

Urogdy’s results were among many findings from Democracy in the Balance: Polarization and the Road Ahead, a spring quarter course taught by Ashley Fabrizio, a Stanford alum and head of research at the nonpartisan think tank More in Common. Working with Fabrizio and her team, students created and conducted a nationally representative survey of 1,610 U.S. adults that oversampled Gen Z to provide a more granular look into their political attitudes and opinions.

Fabrizio, who has taught the course for three years, has found that working with students surfaces concerns that standard polling may miss. “If we want to know what Gen Z’s political beliefs and attitudes are, we should let our students, as members of Gen Z, use their intuition to decide what matters in a survey,” Fabrizio explained.

Working in small groups, students were allocated several minutes of survey time to explore topics such as the political influence of online content promoting masculinity—aka the “manosphere”—the religious revival in Gen Z’s lives, and their beliefs about the American dream. Fabrizio guided students step by step through survey design, showing them how to craft research questions, field the survey, analyze data, and, finally, present their findings.

Students also examined the academic literature on polarization’s effects in American politics, such as how it contributes to political gridlock, drives support for political violence, and erodes trust in American institutions.

“There are many legitimate divisions in politics over competing policies and values, but polarization often drives us apart unnecessarily,” said Fabrizio. “Young Americans will have to find their own ways of bridging partisan differences and overcoming misconceptions about one another. I hope this class helps students see the value of doing so and gives them a sense of agency in addressing polarization.”

Natalia Galperin was excited about the opportunity to run her own study from start to finish, a first for the Stanford undergrad majoring in psychology. She also wanted to expand on her prior work as a research assistant for political scientist Shanto Iyengar in his Political Communication Lab, where she studied the effects of negative political campaign ads.

For her research project, Galperin examined the role of social media in inflating Gen Z’s hostility toward people from the opposing political party, a phenomenon political scientists call “affective polarization.”

“We thought Gen Z would be more polarized and misinformed because we get so much of our news on social media compared to older generations,” Galperin said.

What she and her classmates found reveals a more complicated picture.

While Gen Z respondents who said they used social media daily or almost daily were more likely to dislike the opposing party, their scores were almost identical to those of other generations.

“We found that greater social media engagement is generally linked to more polarized views of political parties, and the effect is seen at similar rates across all generations, not just Gen Z,” said Galperin, who will be interning with More In Common this summer.

Practices to help campus communities connect across lines of race, faith, ideology, and more.

Galperin also wanted to know whether social media deepens the divide between what Gen Z thinks people from the other side believe versus what they actually think, a phenomenon known as “perception gaps.” In testing people’s perceptions on immigration, she found that Gen Z did not appear to hold wildly distorted views about the other side—findings that push back against the familiar narrative that being online warps a person’s perceptions of politics.

Taken together, actively using social media seems to harden Gen Z’s feelings more than it distorts basic facts.

The class also found a wide range of political viewpoints, including differences between Gen Z who identified as Democrats and Republicans.

For example, in Urogdy’s project, he and his teammates found that those who were the most confident that polarization can be reduced identified as conservatives and Republicans, while liberals and Democrats believed the opposite—a finding that Urogdy said tracks with prior research: A person’s view of government depends on whether or not their political party is in control.

Galperin’s team also found lower levels of affective polarization among Republicans and Gen Z overall, and Democrats who reported actively using social media daily have higher perception gaps on immigration-related issues than average.

Another student team’s project revealed further complexities. They found that many Gen Z respondents are more likely than other generations to attribute problems like the affordability crisis to systemic failures in democracy itself rather than to specific policies or leaders. In their data, a notable share of young people said the system itself “is not capable of doing its job,” signaling a deeper, structural disillusionment.

“I think we’re all exhausted by the political system,” Urogdy said. “There’s this underlying feeling that what we want isn’t being translated into tangible change, and I think that there’s this overall feeling that instead of having animosity towards people across the aisle, there’s an animosity towards the system itself.”

Urogdy is pragmatic about what comes next.

“We can’t say polarization will disappear if we will it away,” said Urogdy, who is majoring in political science. Now, he feels he has a better understanding of what kinds of solutions matter. If people are disillusioned with the system, surface-level fixes—such as messaging—won’t last, he said. Efforts need to be ongoing. “If Gen Z is still one of the most reachable generations, the answer is sustained civic engagement, where we can rebuild trust in the system while working to reform it. We have a long path ahead,” said Urogdy, who said he is optimistic.

Fabrizio, too, is hopeful. “Gen Z is inheriting a polarized nation, but they are inheriting deep wells of democratic vitality, as well,” Fabrizio said. “America has a long history of self-government, a robust civil society, and communities that remain deeply committed to democratic values. Gen Z has high standards for our democracy, but living up to them is within reach. I hope older generations will listen and be inspired by Gen Z’s vision for the American dream.”

#9413. The Overlooked Ways Love Shows Up in Urban Spaces

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Over the past two decades, my doctoral students and I have focused on studying love, care, kindness, and compassion in urban settings. Why? Because social science research on life in America’s cities is desperately incomplete. Much like the vision of urban life that permeates most of American popular culture, social science research imagines urban areas as sites of overwhelmedness, disengagement, social and moral crisis, threat, and violence.

But, as someone who has lived and worked in large urban centers—New York City, Chicago, Detroit, Istanbul—I know firsthand that urban centers are also sites of human virtue. People in urban contexts, including those living in high-stress, oversurveilled, underresourced communities, draw daily from deep wells of love, compassion, empathy, kindness, and generosity in the service of caring for each other. From holding doors open for one another, to offering seats on buses and trains, to stopping to help with directions, to paying unexpected compliments, city-dwellers create environments that are saturated with powerful but easily missed acts of care.

My former students and I have been eager to understand how love, generosity, and care manifest and operate in the hyperdiverse, densely populated, loud, fast-paced complexities of urban spaces. Through surveys and interviews, we have sought to understand how adults residing in big cities define love, how they see love being expressed, and their views of the cascading effects of giving and receiving care, generosity, and love.

We have learned that the decision to express love and care for others in large cities is not simply a moral or emotional decision. We offer two examples of the lens needed to notice the presence of love in cities.

First, we have learned that identities matter in experiences of compassion, love, and care between strangers. Urban dwellers’ identity (for example, race or gender), lived experience, context, familial, cultural, and legal systems’ realities work together to shape decisions about whether to extend acts of love to people you do not know. For example, Kehinde, a 26-year-old African American man living in a large, densely populated city, described his experience of giving and receiving kindness, care, and love in his city as shaped by how he navigates other people seeing him as a Black man.

“I will see folks all the time that may need a hand with their bags or crossing the street or just little things like that. And I take a second, hesitate,” Kehinde says. “I don’t want to scare them. I don’t want to come off as a threat.”

To get through these moments, Kehinde describes engaging in a practice of analysis and shape-shifting. Before he steps in to offer help, he assesses the environment and changes the way he carries himself so that people will perceive him as a possible helper rather than as a threat. He says: “I smile a lot more. My voice might change a bit.” He might shrink his body and keep his head down, to avoid seeming intimidating. After helping someone, he moves along without lingering. Reflecting, he acknowledges not being his full, true self in these interactions. “I have to realize I’ve been socialized—made to believe that this is what I need to do in order to navigate the situation.” Kehinde’s story highlights the point that identities matter in economies of care. The images and stereotypes that we construct about people come at a cost even in moments of compassion. Stereotypes affect who we perceive as deserving of care, concern, and protection. Stereotypes also inform our expectations about who can be trusted to help. Stereotyping is not unique to urban settings. But because urban settings tend to be especially diverse spaces, they create abundant opportunities to study how identities and the social scripts we hold affect the way that strangers care for each other across lines of difference. What Kehinde and others bring to the fore is the reality that the targets of stereotyping are aware of the ways that they are perceived. They learn that to be seen as helpful rather than as threatening, they need to read situations correctly, make adjustments to their approaches (e.g., keep “appropriate” distance), and exit situations strategically. Targets of stereotyping must strike a balance between their own deep-seated motivations to behave caringly and their desire to stay safe. For individuals like Kehinde, miscalculations can be costly. If, in the effort to behave lovingly and compassionately, someone is misidentified as a threat, that can lead to a range of consequences from being rebuffed and embarrassed to becoming the target of violence, arrest, or death. The end result is that people consciously or unconsciously learn the rules of engagement around helping strangers.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

A second lesson that has emerged from studying love in urban settings is that love lives in the built environment of cities. I highlight this lesson in my Positive Psychology in Urban Settings classes. Cities are often saturated with murals, billboards, and symbols that convey messages of love, solidarity, and belonging. As residents move through neighborhood streets, they may encounter signs prominently posted in shop windows or near the entrances of religious institutions that remind them that “Black Lives Matter,” “Love Is Love,” or “Immigrants Are Welcome Here.” People display rainbow flags and national flags from apartment windows, on cars, and in other spaces, declaring both their own identities and pride for and solidarity with those identities. The architecture of urban spaces may also play a role in expressions of love and care. In many urban neighborhoods, porches, stoops, and front steps serve as places of connection and care. Simple greetings (e.g., “Morning, baby!,” “You doing good?”) voiced by neighbors sitting on their steps serve as ways of spatializing love, care, and connection in urban landscapes.

I return here to my initial point. Our studies of urban areas are desperately incomplete and will remain incomplete until we more fully examine how various forms of human goodness—including love and care—flourish in urban settings. Likewise, our understandings of love and care will remain underdeveloped until we explore how these experiences emerge in the most densely populated, diverse, complex social structures in which people live. We will truly understand love when we understand how it is titrated through place, context, history, culture, religion, structures of power, identities, and a host of individual and relational factors. Urban centers give us powerful opportunities to know love.

Jacqueline Mattis, Ph.D., is dean of the School of Arts and Sciences at Rutgers University-Newark. She studies human goodness in urban contexts.

#9412. This Vitamin Deficiency May Double Heart Disease Risk

People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.

People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.

A deficiency in vitamin D is linked to a doubling in the risk of heart disease.

After exposure to sunlight, vitamin D is produced in the skin and converted to calcifediol in the liver and then converted to calcitriol in the kidney.

Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) is an active form of vitamin D affecting the immune system, bone growth, the production of adrenaline, noradrenaline, dopamine, and serotonin.

A study suggests that calcitriol can also influence cardiovascular health through its effects on other systems, including the immune system.

In this research, participants with low levels of vitamin D appeared to have higher blood pressure and heart disease risk compared to people with adequate blood levels of vitamin D.

The results showed that people with the lowest levels of vitamin D were twice as likely to suffer from cardiovascular disease than those within the normal range.

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a major cause of death and disability, killing 7.9 million people around the world each year.

Over a billion people globally have low levels of vitamin D.

The best test to determine vitamin D status is measuring the serum concentrations of 5-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D).

To investigate the association between serum 25(OH)D levels and CVD risk, the research team analysed UK Biobank data on over half-a-million participants.

They found that the risk of high blood pressure and heart disease steeply decreased where the serum 25(OH)D level was around 50 nmol/L.

Over 55 percent of participants had serum levels of < 50 nmol/L and 13 percent were deficient with levels below 25 nmol/L.

The number of people with serum levels less than 50 nmol/L has been estimated to be 37 percent for Canada, 24 percent for USA, and 23 percent for Australia.

Professor Elina Hyppönen, the study’s leader, said:

“Severe deficiency is relatively rare, but in settings where this does occur it is very important to be proactive and avoid negative effects on the heart.

For example, deficiency can be a problem for people living in residential care who may have limited exposure to sun.”

Vitamin D can be found in some foods but this amount is not enough.

“We can also get vitamin D from food, including oily fish, eggs and fortified foods and drinks.

This said, food is unfortunately a relatively poor source of vitamin D, and even an otherwise healthy diet does not typically contain enough.

If we don’t get any vitamin D through the sun, this is one of the rare nutrients for which we sometimes need to take a daily supplement to keep up with the requirements.

Understanding the connection between low levels of vitamin D and CVD is especially important, given the global prevalence of this deadly condition.

Our results are exciting as they suggest that if we can raise levels of vitamin D within norms, we should also affect rates of CVD.

In our study population, by increasing vitamin D-deficient individuals to levels of at least 50 nmol/L, we estimate that 4.4 percent of all CVD cases could have been prevented.”

The study was published in European Heart Journal  (Zhou et al., 2021).

#9410. Iraq’s national museum announces reopening after major renovations

The Iraq Museum in Baghdad has been closed for two years for renovations Photo: Hussein A.Al-Mukhtar via Wikimedia

The Iraq Museum in Baghdad, which has been closed for two years for renovations, will reopen on 1 December. Ali Al-Dakhili, Iraq's Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, confirmed that the museum, which was initially scheduled to reopen in January, will now open at the beginning of next month with several new galleries, according to a post on an official government Facebook page last week. The ministry and the museum's director Luma Yas Jasim al-Douri had not replied to a request for comment at the time of publication.

Several important artefacts and specially curated wings have been prepared for public display, according to the newspaper Iraqi News, which obtained an official document about the reopening from the ministry. These include Assyrian statues and reliefs comprising monumental winged bulls (lamassu), stone carvings depicting Assyrian kings and cuneiform collections. The new Abbasid and Islamic galleries will display intricately carved wooden mihrabs and monumental calligraphic friezes, as well as mosaics and stone relics.

The reopening of Iraq’s national museum—which houses tens of thousands of Mesopotamian, Sumerian, Babylonian and Assyrian antiquities and was closed for various periods after it was looted in 2003 during the US-led invasion—is a priority for Al-Dakhili who was sworn in last month as part of the new government under Ali al-Zaidi. In an official statement on 25 October, Al-Dakhili mentioned the museum's importance and added that there are plans afoot for “a new building that befits the historical and civilisational value of Iraq”.

Paul Collins, the keeper of the Middle East Department at the British Museum who has worked with Iraqi colleagues to develop partnerships in support of museums and heritage in the country, tells The Art Newspaper that the reopening of the Iraq Museum “is an important moment, reflecting Iraq’s strong commitment to preserving its world-renowned cultural heritage and promoting heritage tourism”.

According to another Facebook post from the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities—formerly known as the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Antiquities until the tourism portfolio was separated from it in October as part of government restructuring under Al-Zaidi—tourism is seen as a way to attract foreign investment. Recently, dozens of foreign delegations have visited Ur, the site of the Sumerian ziggurat and the birthplace of the Prophet Abraham, located within the Dhi Qar governorate and Nasiriyah where Al Dhakili is from.

A number of museums have opened in Iraq in recent months while new ones been announced. On 15 November, the Abbasid Palace in Baghdad reopened to the public in an official ceremony, according to Iraqi News. Last month, Iraq’s first Jewish museum opened in Baghdad in the restored Shamash Jewish School, which was founded in 1928. The museum displays personal objects, photographs and documents from Iraq’s once prominent Jewish community and pays tribute to prominent Jewish Iraqi figures such as the vocalist Salima Murad and Sassoon Heskel, who served as the modern state of Iraq’s first finance minister.

Ali Al-Dakhili, Iraq's Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, has announced that a new museum will open in the former Presidential Palace in Babylon Photo: Hadani Ditmars

Meanwhile, according to a spokesperson for the World Monuments Fund, the long-awaited reopening of the Mosul Museum, looted in the aftermath of the 2003 invasion and ransacked by ISIS in 2015, will take place next spring.

Al-Dakhili has also announced that the openings of three new museums in Nineveh, Diyala and Diwaniyah governorates are imminent and that “logistical procedures are ongoing to complete the opening of a museum in Babil Governorate within the Presidential Palace” (the former ruler Saddam Hussein’s old palace located within the site of Babylon). The museum will feature “archaeological and heritage collections for the governorate, highlighting its status in the history of human civilisation”, the statement says.

#9409. How To Instantly Read Someone’s Personality With One Question

One type of question can indirectly reveal a lot about a person’s personality.

One type of question can indirectly reveal a lot about a person’s personality.

Asking someone what they think about other people reveals much about their own personality.

The reason is that people tend to see more of their own qualities in others.

The generous person sees others as generous and the selfish person sees others as selfish.

Dr Dustin Wood, the study’s first author, said:

“A huge suite of negative personality traits are associated with viewing others negatively.

The simple tendency to see people negatively indicates a greater likelihood of depression and various personality disorders.”

The conclusions come from a series of three studies.

In one people were asked to judge the positive and negative characteristics of three other people.

The more positively they judged those people, the more happy, enthusiastic, capable and emotionally stable they turned out to be themselves.

People who judged others more positively also turned out to be more satisfied with their own lives.

Set against this, those who judged others more negatively had higher levels of narcissism and antisocial behaviour.

The researchers even returned to the same people a year later and found the results were the same.

This suggests that what people’s ratings of others say about themselves remains stable over time.

Personality disorders are often diagnosed at least partly by how people view others, the authors write:

“…although narcissists may perceive others as being uninteresting or worthless, this may not reflect how they see themselves.

Similarly, individuals displaying behaviors typical of paranoid personality disorder may believe that others are malevolent and untrustworthy, even though they may not see themselves that way.

Machiavellianism is usually measured in part by asking individuals the extent to which they perceive a lack of sincerity, integrity, or selflessness in others’ actions, and narcissistic behavior is thought to be prompted in part by a belief that other people are inferior, uninteresting, and unworthy of attention.”

The study was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (Wood et al., 2010).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9408. Can Artificial Intelligence Predict the Right Partner for You?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Finding love is big business (a multi-billion–dollar industry), and artificial intelligence is transforming that business. Dating apps are increasingly outsourcing user matching to AI. Recent examples range from Overtone, an AI-powered matchmaking service started by the former chief executive officer of Hinge, to SciMatch, a dating app that aims to use AI to detect compatibility from a single selfie. But can AI actually help people find love?

The promise of AI is to go deeper and end the days of endless swiping and unreturned messages. Now people can talk to AI about their hopes, dreams, and ideal partner preferences and AI can scan the pool of dating app users to find candidates who fit those criteria exactly. AI can also track behavior in the app to learn what people really want (something behavioral scientists call revealed preferences).

As a relationship scientist, I see both peril and promise in this new generation of dating apps. Despite long-heralded promises by dating app companies that their apps are based on relationship science, the truth is that there is no strong foundation of science upon which to build these matching algorithms—relationship scientists do not know what makes two particular people compatible with each other. Not yet, anyway. Sure, we know some of the factors that generally predict liking—physical attractiveness, positive personality traits, similarity, familiarity, reciprocity—but we have yet to predict with the kind of certainty dating apps might like to claim whether any two people will hit it off before they even meet.

So if a robust science of compatibility doesn’t exist yet, what is the AI matching based on? One of the first AI dating apps, Fate, uses “similarity and reciprocity of personality,” according to an interview with the founder. That sounds reasonable, and research from Amanda Montoya and her colleagues looking across 313 different studies of similarity and attraction does suggest that similarity may predict attraction—before people meet. Once people experience even a brief interaction, similarity has much less, if anything, to do with how much two people like and are attracted to each other, as seen in an analysis of actual and perceived similarity of personality traits in potential partners, by Sarah Humberg and her colleagues. A systematic inquiry from my research lab, led by Annika From, also yielded little evidence that romantic couples are happier if partners are more similar to each other.

What about “reciprocity of personality”? If this phrase refers to the idea that two people may have complementary personalities that meld well together, this theory of compatibility, unfortunately, has even less empirical support.

Perhaps it is not too concerning that we lack a strong, agreed-upon scientific basis for predicting compatibility. After all, one of the great promises of AI is that it will learn as it goes, based not just on what a user says they want, but how they actually behave (who they swipe right on, whom they actually chat with after matching). Emerging evidence from different fields suggests that AI may be able to detect complex patterns that humans have been unable to discern. In the medical field, AI has been used to create more precise and accurate predictions that are aiding diagnosis and treatment. From weather prediction to fraud detection, the use of AI has enhanced forecasting. So maybe it can do the same for our love lives?

If the problem has simply been that we have not been able to identify the complex patterns that make up human compatibility, then AI may, in fact, be the answer. If, however, the problem is that humans themselves are too complex, then AI may not get us any closer to being able to forecast love.

What do I mean by this? Well, researchers have found that people will list their preferred partner traits before taking part in a speed dating event, only to have all those preferences go out the window when they actually interact with people. In my own work, I have discovered that people will dismiss another user’s dating app profile for reasons like “same name as my brother” and “bad haircut.” Yes, they will rule someone out as the possible love of their life because of something as irrelevant as their name (give them a nickname!) or hairstyle (arguably our most changeable physical characteristic).

Why do I bring up these examples? They raise the question of whether AI even has the right information to rely on when gathering data based on people’s stated preferences or swiping behavior. So what data might AI need? In my lab, we hope to find some answers to this question with a series of studies that aim to combine dating-app data with real-life interactions. This project will allow us to see what chemistry looks like online and offline, uncover who has online chemistry that translates into real-world sparks, and identify the factors that make chemistry more likely between two people (if there are any meaningful predictors).

The truth is, researchers at the forefront of this work do not always agree on whether forecasting love is even possible. While many relationship scientists have devoted their careers to testing the complex ways in which personalities and preferences interact to predict compatibility, they have arrived at different conclusions. Some researchers believe it will be possible to build an algorithm to predict compatibility; these researchers would likely see the promise in AI. On the other hand, there are those who have concluded that compatibility is a dynamic process that evolves as two people interact with each other and cannot be predicted ahead of time. For these researchers, finding love is less about the perfect match and more about being in the right place at the right time and then building love together through shared moments, from special nicknames and in-jokes to regular rituals just the two of you share.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

With the research projects in my lab, we hope to test these theories by having people meet different numbers of times. We’ve seen from our early work that pairing two random people together does not typically produce high levels of chemistry. That instant attraction seems to be relatively rare; but what if they met repeatedly? Could chemistry develop? Does it need some sort of initial spark to set it off, and can we create that spark with the right equipment, such as a well-placed question or activity that brings two people together? In other words, is chemistry possible with anyone if the right conditions were met, or is there some, as yet undiscovered, set of requirements for two people to be able to fall in love?

I don’t know the answer to these questions yet, nor does the field of relationship science, although many have theories. I see AI as both an exciting tool that might help us answer this question as well as a technology that people looking for love should employ with caution. When used as a way to explore and test models of compatibility, AI may yield invaluable insights. But we must always remember that AI is trained with specific beliefs about what makes two people compatible. If researchers do not yet know what makes two people compatible, then letting AI do all the work to vet potential partners means you are only going to see the people that AI thinks are right for you, while likely remaining in the dark about how AI decided they’re a good match. This gap in knowledge may keep you from meeting someone unexpectedly compatible with you.

An alternative approach to dating is to think about it as a time for exploration. Instead of only connecting with people who have similar facial structures or reciprocal personalities, try dating people with all kinds of different experiences, personalities, beliefs, and desires. If you go this route, Paul Eastwick offers a valuable piece of advice in his recent book Bonded by Evolution: for those who have serious dealbreakers (e.g., you know you want children, have strong religious views, or do not eat meat), go ahead and surround yourself with people who share those views. This will help you avoid facing potentially difficult lifestyle tradeoffs in the future if you do find yourself falling in love. But don’t eliminate someone just because of a bad haircut or a shared name. Instead, be open to exploring and then see for yourself who you connect with and who you do not. You might end up being surprised.

Amie M. Gordon, Ph.D., is a social-personality psychologist who takes a dynamic, dyadic approach to investigating the affective, social-cognitive, and biological processes that shape interpersonal relationships. Her research has been published in top academic journals as well as featured in popular news outlets such as The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and The Atlantic. She received her PhD in Social-Personality Psychology from UC Berkeley and her BA in Psychology from UCLA. She blogs for Psychology Today in Between You and Me, and is currently completing a postdoctoral research fellowship at the University of California, San Francisco.

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds

Average savings flying Tuesday or Wednesday vs Friday or Sunday

Optimal domestic flight booking window before departure

Typical per-ticket savings from fare alerts catching price drops

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Airline pricing is driven by demand, and demand follows predictable weekly patterns. Business travelers fly Monday mornings and Thursday or Friday afternoons. Leisure travelers fly Friday evenings and return Sunday afternoons. The days with the least demand — and therefore the lowest fares — are Tuesday, Wednesday, and Saturday.

Here is what the aggregate pricing data from Google Flights, Hopper, and airline fare databases consistently shows:

The savings are most pronounced on popular leisure routes (New York to Miami, Chicago to Los Angeles, any route to Las Vegas or Orlando) where weekend demand is highest. On less popular routes or business-heavy corridors, the day-of-week effect is smaller. The practical takeaway: if you have any flexibility, fly out on Tuesday or Wednesday and return on a Tuesday or Wednesday. A couple flying round-trip can save $100 to $400 simply by shifting their travel days.

One important note: these are averages across thousands of routes. Individual route pricing varies based on competition, seasonal demand, and airline capacity decisions. Always compare specific dates using Google Flights rather than assuming Tuesday is cheapest for your exact itinerary.

The old advice about booking flights on a specific day of the week — typically Tuesday at 1 AM — is a myth that has never been supported by data. Airlines use dynamic pricing algorithms that adjust fares thousands of times per day based on demand, competition, and remaining seat inventory. There is no magical booking day.

What does matter is how far in advance you book. Here are the optimal booking windows based on aggregate data from Hopper, Google Flights, and CheapAir analyses of millions of fares:

The general pattern is that prices start high when flights first open (9-11 months out), drop to their lowest point in the 1-3 month window as airlines compete for bookings, then spike in the final 2-3 weeks as remaining seats become scarce. Holiday travel follows a compressed version of this pattern with higher floor prices throughout.

The most reliable strategy is not to try timing the absolute bottom but to set fare alerts and buy when the price drops to a level you consider a good deal. Waiting for a slightly lower fare risks watching prices climb permanently as departure approaches.

The right tools eliminate the need to manually check prices. Here is what works best and how to use each one:

Fare alerts are the single most effective strategy for the time-constrained FI-minded traveler. Set alerts on Google Flights for every trip you are considering in the next 6 months. You will receive email notifications when prices drop, and you can book immediately without daily searching. This passive approach consistently saves $50 to $300 per ticket.

For those building a travel rewards strategy, credit card travel portals (Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Travel, Capital One Travel) sometimes offer slightly better prices than booking direct. More importantly, points earned through everyday spending can cover flights entirely. A card earning 2x points on all purchases turns $25,000 in annual spending into 50,000 points — enough for 1-2 round-trip domestic flights. The FI approach to travel rewards is not to spend more to earn points, but to redirect spending you would do anyway through a rewards-earning card and let the points accumulate passively.

The single biggest predictor of cheap airfare is not when you book or which tool you use — it is how flexible you are with dates and destinations. Google Flights date grid and Skyscanner everywhere search exist specifically to help flexible travelers find the cheapest options. Being willing to fly on a Tuesday instead of a Friday, or to visit Portugal instead of France, routinely saves 30-50% compared to fixed-date, fixed-destination searches. For FI-minded travelers, flexibility is a skill that pays dividends on every trip.

Tuesday and Wednesday are consistently the cheapest days to fly domestically, with fares typically 15-25% below Friday and Sunday prices. Saturday can also be a good value for departures. The savings are largest on popular leisure routes where weekend demand creates the biggest price swings.

No. The idea that booking on Tuesday at midnight gets you the best price is a myth. Airlines adjust prices thousands of times per day using dynamic pricing algorithms. What matters is booking within the optimal window (1-3 months out for domestic flights) and setting fare alerts to catch price drops.

For domestic flights, 1 to 3 months before departure is the sweet spot. For international flights, 2 to 8 months is optimal. Holiday travel should be booked 2 to 4 months ahead. Booking too early (6+ months for domestic) or too late (under 2 weeks) typically results in higher prices.

Sometimes. Spirit, Frontier, and other ultra-low-cost carriers advertise base fares 40-60% below major airlines but charge separately for carry-on bags ($35-$65), seat selection ($5-$50), and other extras. For a traveler with no checked bag and no seat preference, budget carriers save real money. For families or anyone checking bags, compare total cost including all fees — major airlines are often competitive.

Yes. The cheapest times to fly domestically are January (after the 7th), February (excluding Valentine week), early March, late April, September, October, and early November. The most expensive periods are the weeks around Thanksgiving, Christmas, spring break, and the peak summer window from mid-June through mid-August.

Travel rewards cards earn points on everyday spending that can be redeemed for flights. A card earning 2x points on all purchases turns $25,000 in annual spending into enough points for 1-2 domestic round trips. The FI-aligned approach is to use a rewards card for purchases you would make anyway (groceries, gas, utilities) and let points accumulate passively — never spend more just to earn points.

Finding cheap flights comes down to three principles: be flexible with dates (fly Tuesday or Wednesday for 15-25% savings), book in the right window (1-3 months for domestic, 2-8 for international), and let technology do the searching (Google Flights fare alerts catch drops automatically). Combined with a travel rewards card that earns points on everyday spending, these strategies make air travel significantly more affordable without requiring hours of research. Set your alerts, stay flexible, and book when the price is right.

#9406. Am I Doing This Right? Teen Edition

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Parenting a teen can sometimes make you nostalgic for the early years, when you could still scoop up a frustrated toddler and redirect her with bubbles. In the teen years, sweet hugs can provoke eye rolls; a well-intentioned “How was your day?” may be misconstrued as meddling.

That’s just your teens becoming independent. Decades of research finds that portraying adolescence as a period of “storm and stress” is not only misguided, it’s harmful. In fact, developmental science shows this time of life is better recast as “the breakthrough years.” According to research on over one thousand adolescents by Ellen Galinsky, author and president of Families and Work Institute, there are key messages that teens want to get through to adults:

None of this is easy, of course. Along the way, tough situations crop up, and it’s hard to know what to do. Here are common questions, with answers backed by scientists and their research.

Q: My 16-year-old doesn’t seem to be motivated to do anything beyond hanging out with friends and playing video games. When I bring up the prospect of college, he says he doesn’t care. What should I do?

A: As parents, we want to set our high schoolers up for success. But, at that age, young people are still trying to figure out who they are, what interests them, and what their future looks like. “Identity development and purpose formation are underway, but rarely fully formed by high school,” says Kendall Cotton Bronk, professor of psychology at Claremont Graduate University.

Not finding any answers yet is expected. “Parents need to remind themselves that where their child is at this moment in time isn’t necessarily where they will be in the future,” says Bronk.

To help teens along, encourage them to try different activities at school and in the community, whether it’s, for instance, robotics, the debate team, chorus, improv, or the school paper. Leave it to them to select what to try. Don’t do it for them. Don’t judge their choices.

“While it’s not appropriate for parents to be too directive, they can help their teenager reflect on what they liked and didn’t like and what felt meaningful and not so meaningful about their various experiences,” says Bronk. “Having someone to debrief with can help them deepen their reflection and more quickly identify a purposeful direction.”

Research suggests that when teens are guided by their own interests, free of external pressures, they’re more likely to take charge of their own career development. But when parents are overly involved in their adolescents’ lives, says Bronk, young people don’t have an opportunity to cultivate a sense of agency, and this can make career development planning a big challenge.

Instead of trying to manage their path, says Bronk, parents should simply “be curious.” Ask your child: What interests you? What feels satisfying for you?

“This kind of questioning can scaffold and deepen their young person’s reflections, and reflection is a key component of figuring out what kind of path a young person wants to follow,” she says. “Usually, what holds their interest is something they’re good at and care about, and that allows them to make a meaningful difference in the broader world,” she explains.

Taking advantage of volunteer opportunities can help young people see themselves as useful and discover careers that might interest them—for instance, helping out in a food pantry, animal shelter, a kids sports organization, or hospital. Encourage your teen to ask people he knows about their jobs, what they entail, and what they studied to get there.

Finally, don’t assume that your child’s lack of direction is apathy. Whatever their interest is, “work with it, not against it,” says Bronk. “At the same time, be patient. It may just be the case that they haven’t figured it all out yet. Their timetable may not be the same as yours, but they will eventually get there. Remember, this isn’t a race.”

Q: My 15-year-old seems to be living a separate life. He spends most of his time in his room and has dinner more often with his friends than with us. How can we encourage him to be a part of the family?

A: Seeking independence (while still navigating being dependent on adults) is one of the primary tasks of adolescents as they transition to becoming more self-sufficient into early adulthood.

“I try to get parents to understand that it’s not about them,” says Laurence Steinberg, author of You and Your Adolescent. “The parents didn’t do anything wrong; the child isn’t rejecting them. This is a sign they’re growing up normally. It’s partly wanting to make their own decisions and have their own life, but it’s also wanting emotional independence—to show that they are more than their parents’ kid.”

Chances are a closed door doesn’t mean trouble. Just as most adults don’t want others listening in on their calls, teens don’t want that either. They’re not distancing themselves from you, but simply distancing themselves from being a child.

“There’s nothing the parents can do to stop this from happening,” says Steinberg, a professor emeritus of psychology and neuroscience at Temple University. “And they shouldn’t try.”

That said, spending time with family is also important. To suggest that, say something like, “We want to spend more time with you, but we also know that spending time with friends is important. What’s the best way to catch up with you?” By making the planning of it a collaborative process, your child is more likely to stay engaged. Research suggests that they may even find the activity more enjoyable.

Only rarely is a shut bedroom door cause for concern—for instance, you notice other behavioral changes, such as a drop in grades, a dwindling interest in his usual in-person activities. If you suspect an issue, let your child know that you’re there for him, and that he can get professional help, too.

One last note: If your child is spending most of his time in his room online, setting limits on its own may not be enough, says Jacqueline Nesi, author of the Techno Sapiens newsletter and associate professor of psychiatry and human behavior at Brown University. You’ll also want to discuss with them what you want for him and what he wants.

The evidence also supports “co-viewing” or “co-using” technology with your kids, whether that’s a video game, TV, or an AI chatbot, says Nesi. Using tech together can spark conversation and help parents better understand their kids’ digital lives.

That said, it’s still important for you to protect their sleep and to make sure that they live a life in person. Again, to get their buy-in, decide on screen-time parameters, and replace screen time with in-person activities he might enjoy, such cooking a favorite meal together or an outing with family and friends.

Q: My 17-year-old daughter recently suffered a breakup. How can I help her feel better without intruding?

A: Even if a relationship doesn’t look like a monogamous romantic relationship in adulthood (it may be short, or the partners may not talk to each other very much), these breakups can still be painful. So always take your teen’s romantic activities seriously, as well as the emotions they are experiencing following a breakup, says Emily Bibby, a researcher at the Relationship Development Center at Stony Brook University. Be compassionate, validating, and nonjudgmental. Let her know that she is having a normal reaction to a difficult situation.

Allow space to grieve and vent. “Listen hard to what your child is thinking and feeling,” says Barry Farber, professor of psychology and education at Columbia University Teachers College. “Ask what they’ve learned from the relationship. Framing the relationship as a learning experience, as opposed to a failure, can help nurture resilience and personal growth, and can help her feel more in control and more hopeful about future relationships.”

As Farber and his coauthors point out in a recent study, while time doesn’t necessarily “heal all wounds” (because memories and thoughts can linger), it almost always “softens the blow” when other strategies are also employed, such as talking with a trusted friend or family member. While the study involved mostly white, female adult subjects, the same principle generally applies across ages, genders, and ethnicities. Letting your child know that things will get better can help.

Trying to convince a teen to do anything is difficult, says Farber, so it’s better to simply listen, and then only encourage as opposed to insisting or dictating. Encourage her to engage in activities she enjoys, whether it’s treating herself to an afternoon manicure, going to a concert, or spending time in nature like hiking and walking on the beach. Encourage her to avoid all contact with her ex, both in person and on social media. If one person believes it’s really over, a clean break is usually best, says Farber. Any surge of adrenaline that happens when you see your ex in any form is only temporary, and only makes it harder to get over the breakup.

If sad feelings are impairing day-to-day life—she’s not seeing friends, she’s failing her classes, there’s a dramatic change in eating or sleeping—have her consider seeking help from a mental health professional. “Therapy normalizes the experience,” says Farber. “It helps people find a new narrative when they’re stuck.”

Therapy also gives people an opportunity to share their feelings in a private space and learn evidence-based emotion-regulation skills to improve their mental health and functioning, says Bibby.

This workbook is for a range of practitioners who support parents and caregivers of children between preschool and high school.

If your teen is debilitatingly depressed or harming herself, then advise that she get professional help as soon as possible, such as from her school psychologist, her primary care doctor (for a referral), or a therapist you think highly of.

To help their teen navigate relationships in general, parents can model healthy relationships with not just a partner, but also friends and family members. Teaching your teen effective communication skills and boundary setting early on, in the context of friendships and family relationships, can prove helpful once your teen starts dating, says Bibby, who recently coauthored a research review on romantic relationships and mental health in adolescents.

And as for parents of teens who are just becoming interested in dating, it’s helpful to talk about what healthy relationships look like, emphasizing the importance of mutual respect. “Thinking through what they would do [in different dating scenarios] and how to navigate different challenges that may arise can build confidence when they start dating,” says Bibby.

Q: My 14-year-old has found herself in a friend group that spends a lot of money on expensive clothing and electronics. We don’t approve of these teens and don’t share their consumerist values. How do we prevent our child from becoming materialistic, too?

A: You can empower your teen to make thoughtful, confident choices about money, friendships, and the pressures they face. Try leading with connection rather than control: Talk openly about your family’s values, help them practice setting boundaries, and remind them they do not need to match their friends’ spending to belong or feel worthy. Expensive tastes and social media pressures can be hard to ignore, but your teen can learn to make choices that reflect what matters most to them.

People turn to materialistic things to fill a void, but that’s only a temporary fix, says Lan Nguyen Chaplin, a professor of integrated marketing communications at Northwestern University, and an expert in children’s and teens’ consumer behavior. “They end up in a vicious cycle of wanting and needing more to fill the same void because material things cannot fill real voids.”

In her research exploring materialism in a group of 12- to 18-year-olds, she reported that those with high self-esteem were less likely to have materialistic tendencies. “Parents and peers [are] a source of emotional support and psychological well-being,” she writes. “Supportive parents and peers boost adolescents’ self-esteem, which decreases their need to turn to material goods to develop positive self-perceptions.”

Read this article in Spanish on La Red Hispana, the public-facing media outlet and distribution house of HCN, focused on educating, inspiring, and informing 40 million U.S. Hispanics.

To that end, start at home and help your kids feel good about themselves. Gratitude journals can be a good way to curb materialism, but, of course, asking a teen who is new to journaling to start one can feel like a homework writing assignment if it’s yet another thing they are required to do. Rather, approach it with a light touch. Model gratitude by sharing with your teen who and what you’re grateful for, keep a gratitude journal yourself, or ask them what the high point of their day is.

It also helps to stop tying accomplishments to material things. So, instead of, say, rewarding a good report card with money or sneakers, celebrate the hard work that was put into achieving the good grades over a fun experience together like a movie night at home.

Most of all, spend time with your teen in lighthearted and playful ways, no matter how short. Even a 10-minute car ride can be a good opportunity to connect with them, and also reinforce the good things they have going for them, Chaplin says.

Joanne Chen is a writer and editor in New York City. Her articles on children and parenting have appeared in The Bump, Parents Magazine, and the New York Times.

By focusing on culture, family, and community, Jasmin Brooks Stephens says we can support mental health in Black youth long before crises occur.
